paragraphs.text: (de Cons. Ev. iii. 7.) The Evangelist had above brought down his history, of what was done to the Lord as far as early morning; he then turned back to relate Peter's denial, after which he returned to the morning to continue the course of events, When the morning was come, &c.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: (Chapter 27, verses 1 onwards) Now when morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him, and led him away, and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor. He was not only taken to Pilate, but also to Herod, so that both of them might mock the Lord. And see the eagerness of the priests for evil. They stayed awake all night in order to commit murder. And they handed him over bound to Pilate. For they had this custom, that whoever they had condemned to death, they would hand over to the judge bound.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Observe the evil zeal of the Chief Priests; they watched the whole night with a view to this murder. And they gave Him up to Pilate bound, for such was their practice to send bound to the judge any whom they had sentenced to death.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Hom. lxxxiv.) They did not put Him to death in secret, because they sought to destroy His reputation, and the wonder with which He was regarded by many. For this reason they were minded to put Him to death openly before all, and therefore they led Him to the governor.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: For because they were desirous to put Him to death, but were not able themselves because of the feast, they lead Him to the governor.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: But mark, I pray thee, how the act was forced on, so as to take place at the feast. For so was it typified from the first.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: O religious leaders [of the Jews], this morning was far from your time of ascendency, as it might have seemed to you. Your sun was in fact beginning to set. The dawn you expected did not come. A night of blackest darkness was brooding over your spiteful hearts. Out of this morning would come the overthrow of the temple and its altars, the surpassing of the law and the prophets, the undoing of the kingship and priesthood, turning youth to continual lament. For you set out that morning on a mad and bloody course. You offered up to die the Author of life, the Lord of glory. Pilate—that terror-stricken judge—was overcome by your shouts, so that he chose a man for pardon who was a murderer and demanded the crucifixion of the Savior of the world.
paragraphs.author: Leo the Great

paragraphs.text: But when morning had come, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, that they might deliver him to death; and they led him away bound and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor (27, 1. 2).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He who stumbles in the darkness and at night is worthy of pardon, but he who stumbles in the clear daylight can never blame his error as though it belonged to one who is master of himself (especially when he stumbles while having within himself the "lamp of the body"), but rather he must blame his own lack of self-mastery. Now we have said this to show that the disciples of Christ are indeed scandalized in the night, according to what the Lord foretells to them: "you will all suffer scandal because of me on this night", and because Peter denied three times before the cock crowed. But those who take counsel against Jesus — all the chief priests and elders of the people, when morning had come — sin in the light, that is, knowingly, according to what is written concerning this counsel, that they took counsel with one accord "together", as it is written in the Psalms, that they might deliver Christ to death, thinking to extinguish through his death his teaching and the faith in him among those who had believed in him as in the Son of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But taking such counsel against him, the chief priests of the cult of the letter that kills, and the elders of the ministry of condemnation, bound Jesus, who looses men from their bonds and "says to those who are in bonds: come forth", and who looses those who are fettered and says: "let us break their bonds asunder, and let us cast their yoke from us", and who had loosed from her bonds "the daughter of Abraham" bound by Satan "for eighteen years", so that she who "before could not at all look upward" should now be no longer bent down. And they bound him who willed it, and who, in the very fact that he was bound, was laying an ambush against those very bonds and breaking them, so that now the chief priests and elders of the Jews should have no bonds against men, the Lord evidently breaking them in himself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if anyone requires of me a Scripture showing these things concerning the breaking of the bonds with which the chief priests and elders bound Jesus, let him understand that for this very reason Jesus himself says through the prophet: "let us break their bonds asunder", as if he were speaking of the chief priests and elders, or much more of those rulers who wrought in them, and of the kings of the earth, those who "stood up", and of the princes who "came together as one against the Lord and against his Christ", whose "yoke also let us cast from us". But he will satisfy you still further, so that you may accept that, even though those who took counsel against him led Jesus away bound, nevertheless Jesus broke the bonds, if you consider the things that are written concerning Samson, who was frequently bound and broke the bonds of the foreigners, because he had been a Nazarite of God and had hair full of strength.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: If therefore that man, on account of the strength of the hair which he had on his head, was able to break the bonds of the foreigners with which they had frequently bound him, how much more Christ, who after so many wonders and mighty works which he did, willingly delivered himself over to bonds (lulling to sleep within himself the power of his divinity and consenting to be bound), without doubt broke the bonds surrounding him! Of which bonds the bonds of Samson were the mysteries.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: and they handed him over to Pontius Pilate. But whether both names of the governor also have some meaning fitting the dispensation of the Lord and Savior, or not, is not easy to answer with any finality. For the root terms from which these names are derived may move someone — Pontius and Pilatus; but whether one is rightly moved or not, let each of those capable of it come to consider and know.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: They supposed that by His death they should crush His doctrine, and the belief in Him of those who believed Him to be the Son of God. With such purpose against Him they bound Jesus, Who looses them that are bound. (vid. Isa. 61:1.)
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Though it should be observed that they did not now first bind Him, but before, when they first laid hands upon Him in the garden, as John relates. (John 18:12.)
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: Then seeing Judas, who had betrayed Him, that He was condemned, being moved by repentance, he returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood. He cast away the weight of impiety from the greatness of his greed. Seeing that the Lord was condemned to death, Judas returned the price to the priests, as if he had the power to change the sentence of those who persecuted. Therefore, although he changed his will, he did not change the outcome of his first intention.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But if he who handed over the innocent blood sinned, how much more did the Jews sin, who bought the innocent blood, and by offering a price, provoked the betrayal of the disciple? Let those who attempt to introduce different natures and say that Judas, the traitor, had an evil nature, and could not be saved by election, answer how an evil nature could have repented.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: He cast away the weight of impiety from the greatness of his greed. Seeing that the Lord was condemned to death, Judas returned the price to the priests, as if he had the power to change the sentence of those who persecuted. Therefore, although he changed his will, he did not change the outcome of his first intention.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Judas, when he saw that the Lord was condemned to death, returned the money to the Priests, as though it had been in his power to change the minds of His persecutors.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: This was a charge both against him, and against these men; against him, not because he repented, but because he did so, late, and slowly, and became self-condemned (for that he delivered Him up, he himself confessed); and against them, for that having the power to reverse it, they repented not.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: But mark, when it is that he feels remorse. When his sin was completed, and had received an accomplishment. For the devil is like this; he suffers not those that are not watchful to see the evil before this, lest he whom he has taken, should repent. At least, when Jesus was saying so many things, he was not influenced, but when his offense was completed, then repentance came upon him; and not then profitably. For to condemn it, and to throw down the pieces of silver, and not to regard the Jewish people, were all acceptable things; but to hang himself, this again was unpardonable, and a work of an evil spirit. For the devil led him out of his repentance too soon, so that he should reap no fruit from thence; and carries him off, by a most disgraceful death, and one manifest to all, having persuaded him to destroy himself.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: But mark, I pray thee, the truth shining forth on every side, even by what the adversaries both do and suffer. For indeed even the very end of the traitor stops the mouths of them that had condemned Him, and suffers them not to have so much as any shadow of an excuse that is surely shameless. For what could they have to say, when the traitor is shown to pass such a sentence on himself.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: He brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, and saith, I have sinned in that I have betrayed innocent blood. And they said, what is that to us? see thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: For neither could he bear his conscience scourging him. But mark, I pray thee, the Jews too suffering the same things. For these men also, when they ought to have been amended by what they suffered, do not stop, until they have completed their sin. For his sin had been completed, for it was a betrayal; but theirs not yet. But when they too had accomplished theirs, and had nailed Him to the cross then they also are troubled.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: Hear, ye covetous, consider what befell him; how he at the same time lost the money, and committed the sin, and destroyed his own soul. Such is the tyranny of covetousness. He enjoyed not the money, neither the present life, nor that to come, but lost all at once, and having got a bad character even with those very men, so hanged himself.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: Observe that he repents only when his sin is finished and complete; for so the Devil suffers not those who are not watchful to see the evil before they bring it to an end.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he was condemned, led by repentance brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying: I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood. But they said: What is that to us? See thou to it. And casting down the pieces of silver in the temple, he departed, and going away hanged himself with a noose. But the chief priests, having taken the pieces of silver, said: It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And having taken counsel together, they bought with them the potter's field, for the burial of strangers. For this reason that field was called Acheldemach, that is, the field of blood, unto this present day. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying: And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was priced, whom they priced of the sons of Israel, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Let those answer me who introduce certain fables concerning natures, supposing that they speak the truth and not recognizing that their opinion accuses the Creator of injustice, as one who made certain vessels indeed "unto honor" not by reason of any virtue of theirs leading them to honor, but certain others "unto dishonor" not because of their sins leading them to dishonor. For if Judas was of a perishable nature, how did he take up so great a repentance that he was not overcome by desire of the thirty pieces of silver, for the sake of which he took up the impious audacity of the betrayal?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For if they refer to the property of natures what is said: "a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruits", let them say — unless he breathe forth some goodness, even if not perfectly nor as he ought, Judas being converted: this very thing, that he brought back the thirty pieces of silver, whence is it, and that he said, recognizing his sin: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood, unless it be from a good planting of the mind and from the sowing of virtue, which is sown in every rational soul, which Judas did not cultivate and therefore fell into such a sin? But if any of men is of a perishing nature, without doubt Judas too was rather of a nature of this perishing kind. And this without doubt would seem to have been the case, if, betraying innocent blood, he had either not brought back the money, taking his delight in it, or, bringing it back, had not said that I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if indeed Judas had said what he said after the resurrection of Christ from the dead, perhaps it would plausibly have to be said that the very power of his resurrection compelled him to repent of the deed and to confess his sin. But as it is, as soon as he saw that he had been delivered up to Pilate, being stung with compunction he repented; and perhaps also remembering those things which Jesus had frequently said to his disciples concerning his future resurrection.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Judas therefore, seeing the greatness of his crime, did indeed repent and spoke out of the repentance of his heart, confessing his sin, in that he had betrayed innocent blood, "but he did not repent also according to knowledge", as he ought to have repented. For he supposed that he would anticipate in death his master who was about to die, and would meet him with a naked soul, so that, confessing and imploring, he might obtain mercy. For which reason he himself judged and condemned himself in that he had sinned knowingly, and he did not look to what Job had said, when set in such great disasters: "would that I might be able to kill myself, or to ask someone to do this for me", nor did he see that it does not befit a servant of God to expel himself from this life, but rather to await concerning this too the judgment of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Let us now see whether (that which lies hidden from many … of that passage) by God's granting we may be able to explain what is said: But Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he was condemned, led by repentance brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, and the rest. For if it had been written, after the sentence of Pilate, after he delivered Jesus, scourged with whips, to the Jews that they might crucify him, that Judas had done these things, we should without doubt seek nothing of this kind in that which is said: seeing that he was condemned. But as it is, how did Judas see that he was condemned (for Jesus had not yet been condemned nor questioned by Pilate)?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Perhaps therefore someone will say (doing violence to the text) that by the consideration of his own mind he saw the "outcome" of the matter, that he was condemned, from this, that he beheld him delivered up by the chief priests and the elders of the people. But another will say in this way, that what is written: But Judas, seeing that he was condemned, refers to Judas himself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For when the chief priests and the elders of the people had delivered Jesus to Pilate, then Judas felt his own evil and understood that one who had dared such things was without doubt judged and condemned by God. And perhaps Satan too, who after the dipped bread had entered into Judas, was present with him until Jesus should be delivered to Pilate. But after he had done what he wished, "he departed from him"; and, the devil departing, he understood and saw that, betraying innocent blood, he was condemned by God, and his understanding, being now at leisure and no longer having the devil working within him, was able to understand.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: He was able therefore, the devil departing from him, to receive repentance and to bring back the thirty pieces of silver to those who had given them. And he was able to say, the devil departing, what before the devil departed from him he could not have said; for while the devil was still filling his heart he could not say: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood. But we do not say this, that the devil, departing from any such man, thereafter by no means lies in wait for him. Rather he watches again for the time, whether he may again be able to set himself upon him; and after someone has come to recognize [the devil] even in accordance with his own sin, the devil watches also for the place of a third deception in him.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if it is needful to use examples as well, let us consider in the first epistle to the Corinthians him who "had his father's wife", for in such an evil he could not have been without a great working of the devil. Of which evil he repented, as the Scripture itself testifies, and was made sorrowful with a "sorrow according to God", a sorrow "which works repentance unto stable salvation".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But after he took up such sorrow, the devil set himself upon him again, wishing to exaggerate that sorrow of his beyond measure, so that the sorrow itself should no longer be "according to God", but that, being made more abundant, it might swallow up the sorrowing man beyond measure and beyond what he ought to have sorrowed, and thus Satan might swallow him up in "more abundant sorrow". Foreknowing which, the Apostle gives counsel to the Corinthians that they should confirm "love toward him", stating this as the cause: "lest", he says, "he who is such be swallowed up by more abundant sorrow"; "for we are not ignorant of his devices".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Something similar happened also in the case of Judas, who betrayed Jesus, and according to the likeness of that sorrow "which works repentance unto stable salvation", he too being made sorrowful, after he was led by repentance, brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests, saying: I have sinned in betraying innocent blood. Which very thing belonged to repentance and to saving sorrow; but because he never kept his heart, nor sorrowed wisely, but took up a more abundant sorrow sent under to him by the devil (who wished to swallow him up in "more abundant sorrow"), therefore, bringing back those pieces of silver into the temple, he went away and hanged himself with a noose.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For if, after he brought back the money and confessed that he had sinned in that he betrayed innocent blood, he had not gone away and hanged himself with a noose, but had sought a "place of repentance" and awaited the time of repentance, perhaps he would even have found him who said: "as I live, since I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I think that Judas, understanding also something greater concerning the Savior, cast the thirty pieces of silver nowhere else but into the temple, where he knew the Lord had by his act cast out of the temple "the sheep and the oxen", and had said "to the sellers of doves: take these things hence, and make not my Father's house a house of merchandise". Despairing enough of himself, therefore, because he understood the greatness of his sin, casting those pieces of silver into the temple, he departed and hanged himself with a noose.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But those who took up those pieces of silver wished to observe something lawful, and not to put them into the treasury, where the gifts of the people for the needs of the poor were gathered; for they deemed it impious to put the price of blood into the treasury.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For which reason, taking counsel, they purchased with that money the potter's field, of one who works clay; for they saw that it was more fitting for that money to be spent upon the dead and upon the place of the dead and of burial, since it was the price of blood, than in the treasury or in some honorable need. But because among the places of the dead too there are differences (since many indeed according to their wish are desirably buried in their own ancestral monuments, while some, on account of certain calamities, are frequently buried in foreign monuments), therefore those who took up the price of the blood of Jesus used it for the purchase of the field of some potter, that in it foreign dead might be buried, not according to their wish but earning this according to some adverse chance.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if it is fitting to understand the strangers spiritually also, we say that the strangers are those who unto the end are estranged from God and are strangers to his covenants. Such strangers therefore have an end of this kind, that they should be buried in the potter's field, which was purchased with the price of blood.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the righteous are they who say: "we have been buried together" with Christ "in the new monument which is found hewn in the rock", "in the hewn monument, where none yet of the dead has been laid". But those who unto the end are strangers from Christ and aliens from God will say, without doubt, consequently: "we have been buried together" with the strangers in the field of the potter who works clay, which was purchased with the price of blood, and we are in the field which is named the field of blood.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But since what the evangelist says after these things (then was fulfilled that which had been spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying the things which are written) — this is not found to have been prophesied by Jeremiah anywhere in his books, whether those which are read in the churches or those which are recited among the Jews — but if anyone can know, let him show where it is written. I suspect, however, that either it is an error of the Scripture and Jeremiah is put for Zechariah, or that there is some secret writing of Jeremiah in which it is written.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now such is the text in Zechariah the prophet: "and I will say to them: if it is good in your sight, give me my wages, or refuse them; and they appointed my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: put them down into the furnace, and see if it is genuine, even as I was proved for their sake. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and put them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But if anyone saying this supposes that he stumbles, let him see whether this may be prophesied somewhere in the secret writings of Jeremiah, knowing that the Apostle too brings forward certain writings of the secret books, as he says somewhere: "what eye has not seen nor ear heard"; for in no canonical book is this found set down, except in the secret writings of Elijah the prophet. Likewise what he says: "as Jamnes and Mambres withstood Moses" is not found in the public books, but in the secret book which is entitled the book of Jamnes and Mambres. Whence some have dared to reject the epistle to Timothy as having in itself the text of some secret writing, but they were not able to; but that anyone rejected the first epistle to the Corinthians on this account as spurious, has never come to my ears.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Let the propounders of those fables concerning intrinsically evil naturesa answer me here, whence Judas came to the acknowledgment of his sin, I have sinned in that I have betrayed righteous blood, except through the good mind originally implanted in him, and that seed of virtue which is sown in every rational soul? But Judas did not cherish this, and so fell into this sin. But if ever any man was made of a nature that was to perish, Judas was yet more of such a nature. If indeed he had done this after Christ's resurrection, it might have been said, that the power of the resurrection brought him to repentance.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But he repented when he saw Christ delivered up to Pilate, perhaps remembering the things Jesus had so often spoken of His resurrection. (John 13:27.) Or, perhaps Satan who had entered into him continued with him till Jesus was given up to Pilate, and then, having accomplished his purpose, departed from him; whereupon he repented. But how could Judas know that He was condemned, for He had not yet been examined by Pilate?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: One may perhaps say, that he foreboded the event in his own mind from the very first, when he saw Him delivered up. Another may explain the words, when he saw that he was condemned, of Judas himself, that he then perceived his evil case, and saw that he himself was condemned.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (Hil. Quæst. V. et N. Test. q. 94.) Since the Chief Priests were employed about the murder of the Lord from the morning to the ninth hour, how is this proved that before the crucifixion Judas returned them the money he had received, and said to them in the temple, I have sinned, in that I have betrayed innocent blood? Whereas it is manifest that the Chief Priests and Elders were never in the temple before the Lord's crucifixion, seeing that when He was hanging on the Cross they were there to insult Him. Nor indeed can this be proved hence, because it is related before the Lord's Passion, for many things which were manifestly done before, are related after, that, and the reverse.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Augustine

paragraphs.text: It might have been done after the ninth hour, when Judas, seeing the Saviour dead and the veil of the temple rent, the earthquake, the bursting of the rocks, and the elements terrified, was seized with fear and sorrow thereupon. But after the ninth hour the Chief Priests and Elders were occupied, as I suppose, in the celebration of the Passover; and on the Sabbath, the Law would not have allowed him to bring money. Therefore it is to me as yet unproved on what day or at what time Judas ended his life by hanging.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Augustine

paragraphs.text: The very amount and the destination of the money, which on Judas' remorse was recalled from its first purpose of a fee, and appropriated to the purchase of a potter's field, as narrated in the Gospel of Matthew, were clearly foretold by Jeremiah: "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of Him who was valued and gave them for the potter's field.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: But if he who handed over the innocent blood sinned, how much more did the Jews sin, who bought the innocent blood, and by offering a price, provoked the betrayal of the disciple? Let those who attempt to introduce different natures and say that Judas, the traitor, had an evil nature, and could not be saved by election, answer how an evil nature could have repented.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Serm. 52, 5.) When he says, I have sinned, in that I have betrayed innocent blood, he persists in his wicked treachery, seeing that amid the last struggles of death he believed not Jesus to be the Son of God, but merely man of our rank; for had he not thus denied His omnipotence, he would have obtained His mercy.
paragraphs.author: Leo the Great

paragraphs.text: But they said, What is that to us? that is to say, What is it to us that He is righteous? See thou to it, i. e. to thy own deed what will come of it. Though some would read these in one, What must we think of you, when you confess that the man whom yourself have betrayed is innocent?
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: "You shall not steal:" [Exodus 20:15] for Achan, when he had stolen in Israel at Jericho, was stoned to death; [Joshua 7:1] and Gehazi, who stole, and told a lie, inherited the leprosy of Naaman; [2 Kings 5:27] and Judas, who stole the poor's money, betrayed the Lord of glory to the Jews, [John 12:6] and repented, and hanged himself, and burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out; [Matthew 27:5; Acts 1:18] and Ananias, and Sapphira his wife, who stole their own goods, and "tempted the Spirit of the Lord," were immediately, at the sentence of Peter our fellow-apostle, struck dead. [Acts 5:1-11]
paragraphs.author: Apostolic Constitutions

paragraphs.text: (Verse 5.) But they said: What is that to us? You see. And throwing the silver coins into the temple, he left: and going away, he hanged himself. It availed him nothing to have repented, by which he could not correct his crime. If at any time a brother sins against his brother, so that he is able to amend what he has sinned, it can be forgiven to him. But if his works remain, repentance is taken up in vain with words. This is what is said in the psalm concerning the same most unfortunate Judas: Let his prayer be turned into sin (Psalms 108:7); so that he not only could not correct the wickedness of his betrayal, but also added the crime of his own homicide to the former sin. Here's what the Apostle says in his second Epistle to the Corinthians: 'So that on the contrary ye should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.' (2 Corinthians 2:7)
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But when the Devil leaves any one, he watches his time for return, and having taken it, he leads him into a second sin, and then watches for opportunity for a third deceit. (1 Cor. 5:1.) So the man who had married his father's wife afterwards repented him of this sin, but again the Devil resolved so to augment this very sorrow of repentance, that his sorrow being made too abundant might swallow up the sorrower. Something like this took place in Judas, who after his repentance did not preserve his own heart, but received that more abundant sorrow supplied to him by the Devil, who sought to swallow him up, as it follows, And he went out, and hanged himself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But had he desired and looked for place and time for repentance, he would perhaps have found Him who has said, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked. (Ezek. 33:11.) Or, perhaps, he desired to die before his Master on His way to death, and to meet Him with a disembodied spirit, that by confession and deprecation he might obtain mercy; and did not see that it is not fitting that a servant of God should dismiss himself from life, but should wait God's sentence.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Judas did not die by hanging, but lived on, having been cut down before he was suffocated. And the acts of the apostles show this, that falling head long he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out. This fact is related more clearly by Papias, the disciple of John, and the fourth book of the Expositions of the Oracles of the Lord as follows:
paragraphs.author: Papias of Hierapolis
paragraphs.via: as quoted by Apollinaris of Laodicea, AD 382
paragraphs.work: Catenae Graecorum patrum in Novum Testamentum (AD 1844)

paragraphs.text: Judas walked about in this world a terrible example of impiety; his flesh swollen to such an extent that, where hay wagon can pass with ease, he was not able to pass, no, not even the mass of his head merely. They say that his eyelids swelled to such an extent that he could not see the light at all, while as for his eyes they were not visible even by a physician looking through an instrument, so far have they sunk from the surface.
paragraphs.author: Papias of Hierapolis
paragraphs.via: as quoted by Apollinaris of Laodicea, AD 382
paragraphs.work: Catenae Graecorum patrum in Novum Testamentum (AD 1844)

paragraphs.text: His genitals appeared entirely disfigured, nauseous and large. When he carried himself about discharge and worms flowed from his entire body through his private areas only, on account of his outrages. After many agonies and punishments, he died in his own place. And on account of this the place is desolate and uninhabited even now. And to this day no one is able to go by that place, except if they block their noses with their hands. Such judgment was spread through his body and upon the earth.
paragraphs.author: Papias of Hierapolis
paragraphs.via: as quoted by Apollinaris of Laodicea, AD 382
paragraphs.work: Catenae Graecorum patrum in Novum Testamentum (AD 1844)

paragraphs.text: He hung himself, to show that he was hateful to both heaven and earth.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: (Verse 6.) But the chief priests, having received the silver, said: It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. Truly straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel. For if they do not put money into the treasury, that is, into the storeroom for gifts to God, because it is the price of blood, why is the blood itself being spilled?
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Truly straining out the gnat, and swallowing the camel; for if they would not put the money into the treasury, because it was the price of blood, why did they shed the blood at all?
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: What then did that man? When he saw that he was laboring to no profit, and that they would not consent to receive the pieces of silver, "he cast them down in the temple, and went and hanged himself. And the chief priests took the pieces of silver, and said, it is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, the field of blood, unto this day. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, and they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of Him that was valued, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: Seest thou them again self-condemned by their conscience? For because they knew that they had been buying the murder, they put them not into the treasury, but bought a field to bury strangers in. And this also became a witness against them, and a proof of their treason. For the name of the place more clearly than a trumpet proclaimed their blood-guiltiness. Neither did they it at random, but having taking counsel, and in every case in like manner, so that no one should be clear of the deed, but all guilty. But these things the prophecy foretold from of old. Seest thou not the apostles only, but the prophets also declaring exactly those things which were matters of reproach, and every way proclaiming the passion, and indicating it beforehand?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: This was the case with the Jews without their being conscious of it. For if they had cast it into the treasury, the thing would not have been so clearly discovered; but now having bought a piece of ground, they made it all manifest even to subsequent generations.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: Hear ye as many as think to do good works out of murders, and take a reward for the lives of men. These almsgiving are Judaical, or rather they are Satanical. For there are, there are now also they, that take by violence countless things belonging to others, and think that an excuse is made for all if they cast in some ten or a hundred gold pieces.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85

paragraphs.text: The Chief Priests knowing that they had purchased a murder were condemned by their own conscience; they said, It is the price of blood.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: They thought it meet to spend upon the dead that money which was the price of blood. But as there are differences even in burial places, they used the price of Jesus' blood in the purchase of some potter's field, where foreigners might be buried, not as they desired in the sepulchres of their fathers.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or, the foreigners are they who to the end are aliens from God, for the righteous are buried with Christ in a new tomb hewn out in the rock. But they who are aliens from God, even to the end, are buried in the field of a potter, a worker in clay, which being bought by the price of blood, is called the field of blood.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (App. Serm. 80. 1.) It was brought about, I conceive, by God's providence, that the Saviour's price should not minister means of excess to sinners, but repose to foreigners, that thence Christ might both redeem the living by the shedding of His blood, and harbour the dead by the price of His passion. Therefore with the price of the Lord's blood the potter's field is purchased. We read in Scripture that the salvation of the whole human race has been purchased by the Saviour's blood. This field then is the whole world. The potter who is the Lord of the soil, is He who has formed of clay the vessels of our bodies.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: This potter's field then was purchased by Christ's blood, and to strangers who without country or home wander over the whole world, repose is provided by Christ's blood. These foreigners are the more devout Christians, who have renounced the world, and have no possession in it, and so repose in Christ's blood; for the burial of Christ is nothing but the repose of a Christian; for as the Apostle says, We are buried with him by baptism into death. (Rom. 6:4.) We are in this life then as foreigners.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: (Vers. 7, 8.) However, with a plan devised, they bought a field from that potter, for the burial of strangers, therefore that field was called Acheldemach, which means the field of blood, to this day. Indeed, they acted with a different intention, that they might leave a lasting monument of their impiety from the purchase of the land. But we, who were strangers to the Law and the prophets, have embraced their corrupt practices for salvation: and we find rest in the price of his blood. But the field is called 'figulus' because our potter is Christ.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Also we, who were strangers to the Law and the Prophets, have profited by the perverse temper of the Jews to obtain salvation for ourselves.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: They thought it meet to spend upon the dead that money which was the price of blood. But as there are differences even in burial places, they used the price of Jesus' blood in the purchase of some potter's field, where foreigners might be buried, not as they desired in the sepulchres of their fathers.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or, the foreigners are they who to the end are aliens from God, for the righteous are buried with Christ in a new tomb hewn out in the rock. But they who are aliens from God, even to the end, are buried in the field of a potter, a worker in clay, which being bought by the price of blood, is called the field of blood.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (de Cons. Ev. iii. 7.) But if any one thinks this lowers the historian's credit, first let him know that not all the copies of the Gospels have the name Hieremias, but some simply by the Prophet. But I do not like this defence, because the more, and the more ancient, copies have Hieremias, and there could be no reason for adding the name, and thus making an error. But its erasure is well accounted for by the hardihood of ignorance having heard the foregoing objection urged.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: It might be then, that the name Hieremias occurred to the mind of Matthew as he wrote, instead of the name Zacharias, as so often happens; and that he would have straightway corrected it, when pointed out to him by such as read this while he yet lived in the flesh, had he not thought that his memory, being guided by the Holy Spirit, would not thus have called up to him one name instead of another, had not the Lord determined that it should thus be written.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: And why He should have so determined, the first reason is, that it would convey the wonderful consent of the Prophets, who all spake by one Spirit, which is much greater than if all the words of all the Prophets had been uttered through the mouth of one man; so that we receive without doubt whatever the Holy Spirit spake through them, each word belongs to all in common, and the whole is the utterance of each. Suppose it to happen at this day, that in repeating another's words one should mention not the speaker's name, but that of some other person, who however was the other's greater friend, and then immediately recollecting himself should correct himself, he might yet add, Yet am I right, if you only think of the close unanimity that exists between the two. How much more is this to be observed of the holy Prophets!
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: There is a second reason why the name Hieremias should be suffered to remain in this quotation from Zacharias, or rather why it should have been suggested by the Holy Spirit. (Jer. 32:9.) It is said in Hieremias, that he bought a field of his brother's son, and gave him silver for it, though not indeed the sum stated in Zacharias, thirty pieces of silver.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: That the Evangelist has here adapted the thirty pieces of silver in Zacharias to this transaction in the Lord's history, is plain; but he may also wish to convey that what Hieremias speaks of the field is mystically alluded to here, and therefore he puts not the name of Zacharias who spoke of the thirty pieces of silver, but of Hieremias who spoke of the purchase of the field.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: So that in reading the Gospel and finding the name of Hieremias, but not finding there the passage respecting the thirty pieces of silver, but the account of the purchase of the field, the reader might be induced to compare the two together, and so extract from them the sense of the prophecy, how far it refers to what was now accomplished in the Lord. For what Matthew adds to the prophecy, Whom they of the children of Israel did value, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me, this, as the Lord appointed me, is found neither in Zacharias nor Hieremias.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: It must then be taken in the person of the Evangelist as inserted with a mystic meaning, that he had learned by revelation that the prophecy referred to this matter of the price for which Christ was betrayed.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: (Verse 9, 10) Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, 'And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the value of Him who was priced, whom they of the children of Israel priced, and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me.' This testimony is not found in Jeremiah. But in Zechariah, who is almost the last of the twelve prophets, a certain similarity is mentioned (Zech. 11). And although the meaning does not differ much, nevertheless both the order and the words are different.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: I recently read in a certain Hebrew volume, which a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect offered to me, an apocryphal book of Jeremiah, in which I found the following words written verbatim. However, it seems to me more like a testimony taken from Zechariah: just like the Evangelists and Apostles commonly do, who, omitting the order of words, only present the meaning from the Old Testament as an example.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (in loc.) I have lately read in a Hebrew book given me by a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect, an apocryphal Hieremias, in which I find the very words here quoted. After all, I am rather inclined to think that the passage was taken by Matthew out of Zacharias, in the usual manner of the Apostles and Evangelists when they quote from the Old Testament, neglecting the words, and attending only to the sense.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: This is not found at all in Hieremias; but in Zacharias (Zech. 11:13.), who is the last but one of the twelve Prophets, something like it is told, and though the sense is not very different, yet the arrangement and the words are different.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (ad Pam. Ep. lvii. 7.) Far be it then from a follower of Christ to suppose him guilty of falsehood, whereas his business was not to pry into words and syllables, but to lay down the staple of doctrine.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: This field then is this entire world, in which we who have been dispersed and scattered bear the fruit of good work for the Lord.Yet perhaps you would inquire of me, if the field is the world, who the potter might be who could have the ownership of the world. Unless I am mistaken, the potter is the one who made the vessels of our body from clay. Scripture says of him, "Then the Lord God formed the man from the dust from the earth." The potter is the one who, with the warmth of his own breath, made alive the slimy clay of our flesh and with fiery heat put together the fluid and earthly matter of our bodies.
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: The potter, I say, is the one who fashioned us unto life with his own hands and who is refashioning us unto glory through his Christ. The apostle says, "We are being changed into his likeness from one degree of glory to another." That is to say, we who from our previous condition have broken to pieces because of our own misdeeds are restored in a second birth through the loving kindness of this same potter. We who have been struck by death because of Adam's transgression rise anew through the grace of the Savior.
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text:
Clearly this potter is the one of whom the blessed apostle says, "Will what is molded say to its molder?" And again, "Has the potter no right over the clay to make out of the same lump one vessel for beauty and another for menial use?" For from the same clay of our body God preserves some persons for the kingdom on account of their individual merits and keeps others for punishment.
The field of this potter, then, was bought with Christ's blood for travelers. For travelers, I say, who were without home or country and were cast about as exiles throughout the earth, rest is provided by the blood of Christ, so that those who have no possession in the world might have a burial place in Christ.
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: Who do we say that these travelers are if not very devout Christians who, renouncing the world and possessing nothing in the world, rest in the blood of Christ? For the Christian who does not possess the world utterly possesses the Savior.
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: Christ's burial place then is promised to travelers so that the one who preserves himself from fleshly vices like a traveler and stranger may merit Christ's rest. For what is Christ's burial place if not the Christian's rest? We therefore are travelers, in this world, and we sojourn in this life as passersby, as the apostle says: "While we are in this body we are away from the Lord." We are travelers, I say, and a burial place has been bought for us at the price of the Savior's blood.
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: "We have been buried with him," the apostle says, "through baptism in his death." Baptism therefore is Christ's burial place for us, in which we die to sins, are buried to evil deeds and are restored to a renewed infancy, the conscience of the old person having been dissolved in us for the sake of another birth.
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: (de Cons. Ev. iii. 7.) Matthew, having finished his digression concerning the traitor Judas, returns to the course of his narrative, saying, Jesus stood before the governor.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: They led Jesus to Pilate. And they handed him over to the Roman soldiers. Thus the things announced beforehand by the holy prophets were fulfilled to them. For it says, "Woe to the lawless man. Evil will be his lot according to his works." Just "as you have done, so shall it be done to you. Your retribution will be paid back upon your own head."
paragraphs.author: Cyril of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: To Pilate's question as to whether he was king of the Jews, he answered, "It is as you say." How different was the statement he had made to the priest! When the latter asked him whether he was the Christ, he said, "You have said it yourself." This answer is given to the priest as though pertaining to the past, for in many places the law had foretold the coming of the Christ.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: Or, when asked by the High Priest whether He were Jesus the Christ, He answered, Thou hast said, because He had ever maintained out of the Law that Christ should come, but to Pilate who was ignorant of the Law, and asks if He were the King of the Jews, He answers, Thou sayest, because the salvation of the Gentiles is through faith of that present confession.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 11.) But Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, saying: Are you the king of the Jews? The Jews accuse Jesus of impiety, because they were not even able to find anything false to accuse the Savior.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Jesus said to him: You say so. Thus he answered so as to speak the truth and not reveal his speech to calumny. And notice that although Pilate, who unwillingly pronounced the sentence, answered in part: yet he did not want to answer the priests and rulers, considering them unworthy of his speech.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But observe, that to Pilate who asked the question unwillingly He did answer somewhat; but to the Chief Priests and Priests He refused to answer, judging them unworthy of a word; And when he was accused by the Chief Priests and Elders, he answered nothing.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Thus though it is a Gentile who sentences Jesus, he lays the cause of His condemnation upon the Jews.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Or, Jesus would not make any answer, lest if He cleared Himself the governor should have let Him go, and the benefit of His cross should have been deferred.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Seest thou what He is first asked? which thing most of all they were continually bringing forward in every way? For since they saw Pilate making no account of the matters of the law, they direct their accusation to the state charges. So likewise did they in the case of the apostles, ever bringing forward these things, and saying that they were going about proclaiming king one Jesus, speaking as of a mere man, and investing them with a suspicion of usurpation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: Whence it is manifest, that both the rending the garment and the amazement were a pretense. But all things they got up, and plied, in order to bring Him to death.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: This at any rate Pilate then asked. What then said Christ? "Thou sayest." He confessed that He was a king, but a heavenly king, which elsewhere also He spake more clearly, replying to Pilate, "My kingdom is not of this world;" that neither they nor this man should have an excuse for accusing Him of such things. And He gives a reason that cannot be gainsaid, saying, "If I were of this world, my servants would fight, that I should not be delivered." For this purpose I say, in order to refute this suspicion, He both paid tribute, and commanded others to pay it, and when they would make Him a king, He fled.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: Wherefore then did he not bring forward these things, it may be said, at that time, when accused of usurpation? Because having the proofs from His acts, of His power, His meekness, His gentleness, beyond number, they were willfully blind, and dealt unfairly, and the tribunal was corrupt. For these reasons then He replies to nothing, but holds His peace, yet answering briefly (so as not to get the reputation of arrogance from continual silence) when the high priest adjured Him, when the governor asked, but in reply to their accusations He no longer saith anything; for He was not now likely to persuade them. Even as the prophet declaring this self-same thing from of old, said, "In His humiliation His judgment was taken away."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: At these things the governor marvelled, and indeed it was worthy of admiration to see Him showing such great forbearance, and holding His peace, Him that had countless things to say. For neither did they accuse Him from knowing of any evil thing in Him, but from jealousy and envy only. At least when they had set false witness, wherefore, having nothing to say, did they still urge their point? and when they saw Judas was dead, and that Pilate had washed his hands of it, why were they not pricked with remorse. For indeed He did many things even at the very time, that they might recover themselves, but by none were they amended.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: Mark how He that is ordained by His Father to be the Judge of the whole creation, humbled Himself, and was content to stand before the judge of the land of Judæa, and to be asked by Pilate either in mockery or doubt, Art thou the King of the Jews?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or, Pilate spoke this affirmatively, as he afterwards wrote in the inscription, The King of the Jews. By answering to the Chief Priest, Thou hast said, He indirectly reproved his doubts, but now He turns Pilate's speech into an affirmative, Jesus saith unto him, Thou sayest it.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But Jesus stood before the governor; and the governor questioned him, saying: Are you the king of the Jews? Jesus says to him: You say so. Truly Jesus "did not count it robbery that he was equal to God", and not once but frequently he humbled himself for the sake of men. And now therefore, having been "appointed judge of all creation" by the Father, the King of kings and Lord of lords, see to how great a degree he humbled himself, so that he consented to stand before the judge of the land of Judea at that time, and being summoned he was questioned with a question which Pilate perhaps in derision or in doubt asked, saying: Are you the king of the Jews? To which question he answered what he thought fitting, saying You say so. And when he was put on oath by the high priest, that he should say whether he himself is the Christ the Son of God, he answered: "You have said it", but when questioned by Pilate Are you the king of the Jews? he answered You say so. Consider the questions: was not that question, "whether you are the Christ the Son of God", suited to a Jewish person, whereas to the Roman judge saying interrogatively no longer: You are the Christ, but: Are you the king of the Jews?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But whoever carefully considers the very fine points of the Gospel words will see that the high priest indeed said doubtingly: "if you are the Christ the Son of God" (for the syllable "if" shows the doubt of the questioning), but Pilate said declaratively: You are the king of the Jews. And that Pilate said this declaratively, this too is confirmed by the fact that he also elsewhere inscribes above, in the title, "King of the Jews" in three languages, "in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin", so that both Hebrews and Greeks and Romans might know that Pilate too knew him to be the king of the Jews. For which reason it appears with what reverence he inquired concerning Jesus and appealed to the people, that they should ask rather for Jesus to be released than Barabbas. And it was also a sign of Pilate's reverence, that washing his hands he said: "I am innocent of the blood of this man; see you to it".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But that he said to the high priest "you have said it", obliquely reproving his doubt, he refutes it, and that he says to Pilate you say so, he confirms the opinion of the one making a declaration. But Mark, instead of "if you are the Christ the Son of God", writes thus: "are you the Son of the Blessed?" Perhaps either that which is written simply, or this which is written doubtingly — I do not know whether the copies may not have an error, since both ought equally to have said: "if you are", or both: "you are".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For Him it behoved to be made a sacrifice on behalf of all Gentiles, who "was led as a sheep for a victim, and, like a lamb voiceless before his shearer, so opened not His mouth" (for He, when Pilate interrogated Him, spake nothing); for "in humility His judgment was taken away: His nativity, moreover, who shall declare? "Because no one at all of human beings was conscious of the nativity of Christ at His conception, when as the Virgin Mary was found pregnant by the word of God; and because "His life was to be taken from the land.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: (de Cons. Ev. iii. 8.) Luke explains what were the accusations alleged against Him, And they began to accuse him, saying, We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ a King. (Luke 23:2.) But it is of no consequence to the truth in what order they relate the history, or that one omits what another inserts.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: Neither then nor now did Jesus make any reply to their accusations, for the word of God was not sent to them, as it was formerly to the Prophets. Neither was Pilate worthy of an answer, as he had no fixed or abiding opinion of Christ, but veered about to contradictory suppositions. Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders of the people, he answered nothing. Then Pilate says to him: Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you? And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled exceedingly.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The ministers of the Jewish letter that kills, and the elders, are the sons of those priests and elders who accused Jesus, taking up their accusation even until now and accusing Jesus. Therefore, since that very sin remains in them, and "wrath, even to the end" has once forestalled them, they still suffer those same workings, being abandoned along with the whole people "like a tent in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber-field, and like a city that is stormed." And just as Jesus, when accused, then answered nothing, so also now against the accusations of those priests and elders he answers nothing. For the Word of God is silent toward them, and they no longer hear the Word of God, as had once come to pass with the prophets, and, in the consummation of the ages, when he "was made flesh and dwelt among us."
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And not only to the chief priests and elders of the people falsely accusing him did he not respond,
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: but neither to Pilate, since he wished to hear him defending himself against their lying accusations. For when Pilate said to him, after the accusations of the chief priests and elders: Do you not hear how many things they accuse you of?—
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: not even to him did he respond. For it was not fitting to respond even to one who was in doubt as to whether he ought to respond against their false accusations.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: This we have said not forgetting what was said about Pilate, namely that he had at least some momentary kindly disposition toward Christ (for that this is true of Pilate is shown from the whole narrative concerning him).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Yet no one will dare to say that the judgment about Christ within him was abiding and firm; for he was being drawn also to the contrary. Therefore now too, to one being drawn toward the worse opinion, the Lord did not respond, despising all the things that had been said in accusation of him.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But Pilate marveled at his constancy, perhaps knowing how, though he was competent to pronounce sentence and to remit the charge … he marveled, seeing him stand in the calm and quiet gravity of wisdom and, with judgment, unperturbed—he in whom it was reckoned by those who were there that he was in peril of death; and he was stronger than human nature,
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: and, though all its weakness sought to blunt the power of his spirit, it did not prevail to do this.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But the fact that it is written that Pilate did not only marvel, but even marveled exceedingly, moves me to reckon that it seemed to him worthy of great wonder that Christ, when brought forward to a criminal trial, should remain unperturbed and stand before death, which among all men is reckoned terrible.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (Verse 13 and following) Then Pilate said to him: Do you not hear how many testimonies they speak against you? And he did not respond to him with any word, so that the governor wondered greatly. Now it was customary for the governor to release one prisoner to the people on the solemn day, whom they desired. Indeed, it is a Gentile who condemns Jesus, but he refers the matter to the Jewish people. Do you not hear how many testimonies they speak against you? But Jesus refused to respond, in order to not diminish the accusation from the governor, and to prevent the delay of the usefulness of the cross.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: What then saith Pilate? "Hearest thou not how many things these witness against thee?" He wished that He should defend Himself and be acquitted, wherefore also he said these things; but since He answered nothing, he devises another thing again.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: Of what nature was this? It was a custom for them to release one of the condemned, and by this means he attempted to deliver Him. For if you are not willing to release Him as innocent, yet as guilty pardon Him for the feast's sake.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: Seest thou order reversed? For the petition in behalf of the condemned it was customary to be with the people, and the granting it with the rulers; but now the contrary hath come to pass, and the ruler petitions the people; and not even so do they become gentle, but grow more savage and bloodthirsty, driven to frenzy by the passion of envy. For neither had they whereof they should accuse Him, and this though He was silent, but they were refuted even then by reason of the abundance of His righteous deeds, and being silent He overcame them that say ten thousand things, and are maddened.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 86

paragraphs.text: It might seem remarkable to you, brothers, that the Lord should be accused by the chief priests before the procurator Pilate and should be silent and that he should not refute their wickedness by his response, since indeed a defense which follows quickly is the only way to refute a persistent accusation. It might seem remarkable, I say, brothers, that the Savior should be accused and should remain silent. Silence is occasionally understood as avowal, for when a person does not wish to respond to what is asked of him he appears to confirm what is raised against him. Does the Lord then confirm his accusation by not speaking?
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: Clearly he does not confirm his accusation by not speaking; rather he despises it by not refuting it. For one who needs no defense does well to keep silent, but let one who fears to be overcome defend himself and one who is afraid of being vanquished hasten to speak. When Christ is condemned, however, he also overcomes, and when he is judged he also vanquishes, as the prophet says: "that you should be justified in your words and should vanquish when you are judged." Why was it necessary for him therefore to speak before being judged, when for him judgment was a complete victory?
paragraphs.author: Maximus of Turin

paragraphs.text: The governor marvelled at His endurance, as knowing that he had power to condemn Him, He yet continued in a peaceful, placid, and immovable prudence and gravity. He marvelled greatly, for it seemed to him a great miracle that Christ, produced before a criminal tribunal, stood thus fearless of death, which all men think so terrible.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now at the feast day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner, whomever they wished.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Do not be surprised if, the Roman rule still being in its beginnings among them, and the Jews newly taking up the yoke of the Romans, since it had been granted to the Jews that at the paschal solemnity they might ask for one whom they wished,
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: even though he seemed liable for a thousand murders. For thus the nations render certain favors to those whom they subject to themselves, until their yoke is confirmed over them. Yet this custom of releasing a prisoner existed at one time also among the Jews. For when Saul had decreed that no one should take food, but Jonathan had tasted a honeycomb against the king's decree, he found Jonathan liable; and although he was his appointed son, yet on account of some oath of his he had decreed to put him to death. But he did not kill him, since all the people of Israel intervened and asked for him to be granted his life.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But that Pilate released one prisoner to the people, or that Saul, at the people's request, released Jonathan, is no wonder; for the life of both those who were asking was under fault, since the Jews were always liable. But let us inquire whether something of this sort happens also in the judgment of God, so that the whole Church may be able to ask that some sinner be freed from the condemnation of sin — and especially if perhaps he has all the remaining works of perdition, yet is unwearied in doing good to the Church.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For you will find such men often set in positions of power: sinners indeed in other respects, yet doing much on behalf of Christians as far as it is possible for them. And you will be led the more to inquire into such matters, if it has a fitting rationale, seeing that Israel too used to pray to God "for the life of Nebuchadnezzar" and of Belshazzar his son. But this, if it seems to anyone worthy of inquiry, let him inquire into it. But as for what is plain, let us all try to take care that we be found to be among those who ask, and in the rank of those who have lived well, rather than among those on whose behalf petition is made as for evil men. For even if one of the sinners is granted to the prayers of the Church, it is nevertheless not just that such a one should attain glory and blessedness; for it is enough that he be released from punishment.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I think, on account of that festival of the Jews on which Barabbas was chosen for life while Christ was neglected, the Lord says through the prophet: "my soul hates your fasts and your holidays and your feast days". And because they preferred to keep the solemnity with the robber set free rather than with Jesus, I will speak by way of example: if they had kept the solemnity rightly, like Josiah or someone similar to him, and there had been given to them the liberty of asking for whomever they wished, without doubt they would have demanded Jesus and condemned Barabbas. But let us pray that, as we keep the festal day, "not in the old leaven nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth", we may deserve indeed to condemn Barabbas, but to receive Jesus, free from all bonds, as our king and lord. And as long as we do these things, our festal days will not be turned into mourning, nor our songs into lamentation, but there will be in us true solemnities, the solemnities of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Thus do the Gentiles show favours to those whom they subject to themselves, until their yoke is riveted. Yet did this practice obtain also among the Jews, Saul did not put Jonathan to death, because all the people sought his life. (1 Sam. 14.)
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: At that time he had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Now, in the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, 'the son of their teacher' is interpreted as referring to this man, who had been condemned for sedition and murder.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: In the Gospel entitled 'according to the Hebrews,' Barabbas is interpreted, 'The son of their master,' who had been condemned for sedition and murder.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And he sought to rescue Christ by means of this practice, that the Jews might not have the shadow of an excuse left them. A convicted murderer is put in comparison with Christ, Barabbas, whom he calls not merely a robber, but a notable one, that is, renowned for crime.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Now at that time they had a notorious prisoner, who was called Barabbas. So when they were gathered together, Pilate said to them: Whom do you wish that I release to you, Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: In many copies it is not contained that Barabbas was also called Jesus, and perhaps rightly so, that the name of Jesus might not belong to any of the wicked. For in so great a multitude of the Scriptures we know of no Jesus who was a sinner, whereas in other names we find that, among the righteous, there are also found wicked men of the very same name — for instance, Judas the apostle, the zealot, and likewise Judas the patriarch, and Judas Maccabaeus, all praiseworthy, but also Judas the traitor; and in Genesis there are found sons of Seth and sons of Cain bearing the same name, such as Enoch and Lamech and Methuselah.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But it was not fitting that there should be any such thing also in the name of Jesus. And I think that in the heresies some such thing has been added on, so that they might have something apt to say for their fables about the likeness of the name of Jesus and Barabbas. For I judge that in these matters some mystery is set forth: that Barabbas was appointed for sedition and wars and murders to be committed in the souls of men, but Jesus, as the Son of God and peace, was appointed, and as the Word and Wisdom, for all good things.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: These two, then, being bound in human affairs and bodies, that people demanded for itself that Barabbas be released; on whose account that nation does not cease to have seditions and murders and robberies — according to some of that nation in the things that are held outwardly, but according to all the Jews who do not believe in Jesus, inwardly in the soul. For where Jesus is not, there are seditions and quarrels and battles; but where Jesus is, so that they can say: "but if Christ is in us, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness", there all good things are together, and innumerable spiritual riches are in his hands, and peace; "for he himself is our peace, who has made both one". And if anyone should behold that contrary operation, he will recognize that it is he who is in men the bound notorious Barabbas, whom they desire to be released for themselves — not only Israel then sinning according to the flesh, but also all who are like him either in doctrine or in life. Whoever, therefore, does evil things, in his body Barabbas is released, but Christ is bound; but whoever does good things, to him Christ is released, but Barabbas is bound.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them: Whom do you want me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew that they had handed Him over out of envy. Pilate offers them the option of releasing whoever they want, either the robber or Jesus, not doubting that they would choose Jesus, knowing that He had been handed over out of envy. Therefore, the evident cause of the cross is envy.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Pilate gives them the choice between Jesus and the robber, not doubting but that Jesus would be the rather chosen.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Whom will ye that I release unto you? &c. As much as to say, If ye will not let him go as innocent, at least, yield Him, as convicted, to this holy day. For if you would have released one of whose guilt there was no doubt, much more should you do so in doubtful cases. Observe how circumstances are reversed. It is the populace who are wont to petition for the condemned, and the prince to grant, but here it is the reverse, the prince asks of the people, and renders them thereby more violent.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Thus it is plainly seen how the Jewish people is moved by its elders and the doctors of the Jewish system, and stirred up against Jesus to destroy Him.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: John explains what their envy was, when he says, Behold, the world is gone after him; (John 12:19.) and, If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him. (John 11:48.) Observe also that in place of what Matthew says, Jesus, who is called Christ, Mark says, Will ye that I release unto you the King of the Jews? (Mark 15:9.) For the kings of the Jews alone were anointed, and from that anointing were called Christs.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: Whence it is written, "From the beginning the Word was with God, and the Word was God; " to whom "is given by the Father all power in heaven and on earth." "The Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment to the Son" -from the very beginning even.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: (Verse 19 onwards) Now while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying, 'Have nothing to do with that righteous Man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of Him.' But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitudes that they should ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them, 'Which of the two do you want me to release to you?' They said, 'Barabbas!' Note that God often reveals dreams to the Gentiles; and that the testimony of the people is that Pilate and his wife confess the righteous Lord.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Observe also that visions are often vouchsafed by God to the Gentiles, and that the confession of Pilate and his wife that the Lord was innocent is a testimony of the Gentile people.
paragraphs.author: Jerome
