paragraphs.text: But whether any of his garments was torn apart in that division, or whether each of them remained whole as it had been, and what kind those garments were, we do not read in the three evangelists; but in John we learn that "the soldiers, after they had crucified Christ, took his garments and made four parts, to each soldier a part, but the tunic, since it was not sewn together but woven from the top throughout the whole, they said to one another: let us not tear it apart, but let us cast lots for it". Not all of them, therefore, received it, but only the one who obtained it by lot. And if someone were to discuss the difference between those who possess the garments of the Lord, he will without doubt find that there are some who, in their doctrines, even though they do not possess him, nevertheless possess the "tunic" woven from the top "throughout the whole", while others possess not even this but only some small portion of his garment.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And consider this, that according to Matthew indeed Jesus, taking "vinegar mixed with gall", tasted it and "would not drink", but according to Mark, when "wine mingled with myrrh was given to him", "he did not take it".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or, according to the practical exposition, the cross in respect of its broad transverse piece signifies the joy of him that works, for sorrow produces straitness; for the broad part of the cross is in the transverse beam to which the hands are fastened, and by the hands we understand works. By the upper part to which the head is fastened is denoted our looking for retribution from the supreme righteousness of God. The perpendicular part on which the body is stretched denotes endurance, whence the patient are called 'long-suffering.' (longamines) The point that is fixed into the ground shadows forth the invisible part of a sacrament.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: (Verse 36.) And they kept watch over him while he was sitting. The diligence of the soldiers and priests helps us so that the greater and more evident power of his resurrection may appear.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: It proceeds, And sitting down, they watched him there. This watchfulness of the soldiers and of the Priests has proved of use to us in making the power of His resurrection greater and more notorious.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And sitting down they kept watch over him there. And the soldiers indeed kept watch over the body, having been assigned by the chief priests, as though it were liable to be stolen away by his disciples if it were not guarded; but the divine dispensation raised him up and made not only two or three to be witnesses of his resurrection, but far more. For "he was seen by Cephas, then by the eleven, then he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at once", "and last of all" by Paul. And it was no small sign of his resurrection, that he was seen by so many — by those who took up the danger of proclaiming him alive among the peoples who had demanded him for the cross.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And now new chief priests (namely the sons of those chief priests) crucify the word of truth set down in the Scriptures by their false expositions, and slay it with lies; but the word of truth, because among them indeed it is slain yet lives in its own nature, always finds and chooses for itself vessels in which it may rise again and live and still confound its own slayers, shown by many testimonies to be alive.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (Verse 37.) And they placed over his head the charge against him, written, 'This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.' I cannot sufficiently admire the magnitude of the matter, that, for the sake of the redeemed, with a false accusation and having incited the unfortunate people to sedition and outcry, they found no other cause for his execution except that he was the King of the Jews. And perhaps they did this in mockery and ridicule. However, Pilate also responded unwillingly, 'What I have written, I have written.' Whether you want it or not, Jews, a crowd of all nations responds to you: Jesus is the king of the Jews, that is, the emperor of believers and confessors.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And they set up over his head his accusation written, This is Jesus, the King of the Jews. I cannot sufficiently wonder at the enormity of the thing, that having purchased false witnesses, and having stirred up the unhappy people to riot and uproar, they found no other plea for putting Him to death, than that He was King of the Jews; and this perhaps they set up in mockery.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: The High Priest also in obedience to the letter of the Law wore on his head the writing, 'Holiness to the Lord,' but the true High Priest and King, Jesus, bears on His cross the title, This is the King of the Jews; when ascending to His Father, instead of His own name with its proper letters, He has the Father Himself.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And they placed above his head his charge written out: this is Jesus, the king of the Jews.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: "Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed," and every script bears witness to his kingdom, whether of the Greeks or of the Romans or of the Hebrews, and for a crown above his head let there be written: this is Jesus, the king of the Jews, and let no other cause of his death be found (for indeed there was none), let this alone be held: that he was king of the Jews, concerning which he also spoke, saying: "but I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain"; and the chief of the priests indeed, according to the letter of the law, bore upon his head the shape of a sign, "the sanctification of the Lord" written on the plate, but the true chief of the priests and king, Jesus, on the cross indeed has written: this is the king of the Jews, yet ascending to the Father and receiving the Father into himself, in place of letters and in place of a name he has him who is named, and he has him as a crown, having been made worthy of him and made a house worthy of God the Father, he alone can sufficiently contain the Father.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For because He is at once King and Priest, when He would offer the sacrifice of His flesh on the altar of the cross, His title set forth His regal dignity. And it is set over and not beneath the cross, because though He suffered for us on the cross with the weakness of man, the majesty of the King was conspicuous above the cross; and this He did not lose, but rather confirmed, by the cross.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: It was divinely provided that this title should be set up over His head, that the Jews might learn that not even by putting Him to death could they avoid having Him for their King; for in the very instrument of His death He not only did not lose, but rather confirmed His sovereignty.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: Or otherwise; Two thieves are set up on His right and left hand, to signify that the entire human race is called to the Sacrament of the Lord's Passion; but because there shall be a division of believers to the right, and unbelievers to the left, one of the two who is set on His right hand is saved by the justification of faith.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 38.) Then they crucified him with two thieves, one on his right hand, and one on his left. If Golgotha is the hill of Adam and not the place of the condemned, and therefore the Lord is crucified there to raise up Adam, why are the two thieves crucified in that same place?
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: As Christ was made for us a curse of the cross, so for the salvation of all He is crucified as guilty among the guilty.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (Serm. 55, 1.) Two thieves were crucified with him, one on the right hand and one on the left, that in the figure of His cross might be represented that separation of all mankind which shall be made in His judgment. The Passion then of Christ contains a sacrament of our salvation, and of that instrument which the wickedness of the Jews provided for His punishment, the power of the Redeemer made a step to glory.
paragraphs.author: Leo the Great

paragraphs.text: Then they crucified with him two robbers, one on the right and one on the left.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The Lord, crucified among robbers like the robbers themselves, fulfilled the prophecy that says of him: "and he was reckoned among the wicked".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And it is possible to see his disciples, giving testimony to the worship of God which was introduced through him, being reckoned "among the wicked" and being crucified with them, or enduring the remaining sufferings, just as those men did. For the world and the spirit that is in it always persecutes the highest men and punishes indeed the highest in wickedness for the benefit of the many, but the highest in virtue, because this world is not worthy of those who consider not "the things that are seen", but "the things that are not seen", and who despise it, just as also of old the saints walked "in sheepskins and in goatskins, destitute, afflicted, wandering in deserts, in mountains, and in caves, and in the dens of the earth, of whom the world was not worthy".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The thief who was saved may be a sign of those who after many sins have believed on Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: (ap. Gloss. ord.) Or, by the two thieves are denoted all those who strive after the continence of a strict life. They who do this with a single intention of pleasing God, are denoted by him who was crucified on the right hand; they who do it out of desire of human praise or any less worthy motive, are signified by him who was crucified on the left.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: They revile him because they passed by that way, and would not walk in the true way of the Scriptures. They wagged their heads, because they had just before shifted their feet, and stood not upon a rock.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But nevertheless not even here doth their contumely stop, but after having stripped and crucified Him, and offered Him vinegar, they proceeded still further, and beholding Him impaled upon the cross, they revile Him, both they themselves and the passers by; and this was more grievous than all, that on the charge of being an impostor and deceiver He suffered these things, and as a boaster, and vainly pretending what He said. Therefore they both crucified Him publicly, that they might make a show of it in the sight of all; and therefore also they did it by the hands of the soldiers, that these things being perpetrated even by a public tribunal, the insult might be the greater.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: And as they passed by they blasphemed him, wagging their heads and saying: aha, you who were destroying the temple and rebuilding it in three days; free yourself, if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross. Likewise also the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and the elders and the Pharisees, said: he saved others, himself he cannot save; if he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross and we believe him. He trusts in God; he will free him now if he wills him; for he said, that I am the Son of God.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: No one who stands blasphemes Jesus, nor anyone who walks aright; for it was those passing by who blasphemed him (or, as the Greek has it, those going past), who also, once the fence of the vineyard has been broken down by God, gather as their vintage those who have remained; for it is written: "Why have you cast down its fence, and all who pass by the way gather it as their vintage?" So long, therefore, as anyone has not passed by the way nor turned aside from the way, or, standing, can say to God: you have set "my feet upon a rock", he does not blaspheme Jesus; but if he has fallen or gone past or crossed over or turned aside, then he blasphemes him. As, further, those who have fallen into evil works, and those who have forsaken "the eternal bounds" and the way of the heavenly church, and are tossed and carried about "by every wind of doctrine in the deceit of men, in craftiness for the contriving of error".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For if anyone should say that all heresies are passing by and turning aside, he will not sin, for which reason they too are counted among those passing by and blaspheme Jesus, having no firm head, but wagging it up and down, since they are not prudent nor have their eyes in their head, in which they ought to have had them, as the Preacher (Ecclesiastes) says: "the eyes of the wise man are in his head". It is, therefore, the work of those passing by and turning aside to blaspheme Jesus the Son of God, because "no one speaking in the Spirit of God says: anathema to Jesus".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now there are various sayings of the blasphemers, one blasphemy of which is that which is uttered by those who neither understand nor hear the things that are said nor concerning what they make their assertions: for Jesus said: "destroy this temple, and I in three days will raise it up", but those passing by, as "false witnesses" against Jesus, said what had not been said concerning him, assailing him: aha, you who destroy the temple of God, and in three days rebuild it. For he does not himself destroy the temple, but what others destroy he himself builds; whether "the temple of his own body", which had been handed over to death by the Jews, or the temple of his witnesses and of all who had the word of God in them and died from the ambushes of the impious on account of their piety (for "the hour comes when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will rise again"). And not only in that which they said: he who destroys the temple, did they lie, but also in that which they said: "and I in three days will rebuild it". For neither did he say that he would rebuild the temple, but that he would raise it up; for the word of building does not indicate a sudden work, but the word of raising up does indicate it.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And those indeed who were deriding him said save yourself, but he (receiving power from the Father) both did this and more: for to all who receive his word he showed his salvation.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And they indeed, deriding, said: if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross, but he did not show himself the Son of God to those deriding him, yet he showed it to those believing in him, after he had dispensed the things which it behooved him to dispense in those three days, after, descending to the lower regions "put to death in the body but made alive in the spirit, he preached to the spirits who were in prison, who had not believed at some time, when the patience of God was awaited in the days of Noah while the ark was being built, in which few, that is eight souls, were saved through water". And he was not left there (as he himself said: "for you will not leave my soul in hell"), but it behooved him both to ascend to his own Father and God, that "ascending on high" he might take captivity captive and receive "gifts among men", and after these things show himself stronger than death, saying to it: "where, O death, is your sting?"
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And likewise (while the rest were passing by and blaspheming him) the chief priests too and the scribes, themselves also passing by, said to him, overcome by the mighty works done by him before: he saved others, himself he cannot save (clearly not believing that he who was able to save others was much more able to save himself as well), and they promised that they would believe in him as in the King of Israel, if he were seen by them coming down from the cross. But he did not care to do anything unworthy on account of the injury of derision, nor to do what was being said by them apart from reason and order.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Had He then been prevailed on by their taunts to leave the cross, He would not have proved to us the power of endurance; but He waited enduring their mockery; and He who would not come down from the cross, rose again from the tomb.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: What forgiveness then for them, when by the resurrection of His body they shall see the temple of God rebuilt within three days?
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 39 seqq.) And those passing by were blaspheming him, shaking their heads, and saying, 'Vah! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself; if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.' Similarly, the chief priests, mocking with the scribes and elders, said, 'He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him; for he said, "I am the Son of God."' But he, mocking, says that the foolish people had produced false witnesses.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: The foolish rabble cast the same taunt against Him that the false witnesses had invented, Aha! thou that destroyest the temple of God and rebuildest it in three days.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And as beginning to extenuate His former miracles, they add, Save thyself; if thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (Hom. de Cruc. et Latr. ii.) But He, on the contrary, does not come down from the cross, because He is the Son of God; for He therefore came that He might be crucified for us.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: And yet who would not have been moved by the multitude that was following Him, and lamenting Him? Nay, not these wild beasts. Wherefore also He to the multitude vouchsafes an answer, but to these men not so. For after having done what they would, they endeavor also to injure His honor, fearing His resurrection. Therefore they say these things publicly, and crucified thieves with Him, and wishing to prove Him a deceiver, they say, "Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days come down from the cross." For since on telling Pilate to remove the accusation (this was the writing, "The king of the Jews"), they prevailed not, but he persevered in saying, "What I have written, I have written," they then endeavor by their derision of Him to show that He is not a king.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: (Serm. 55. 2.) From what source of error, O Jews, have ye sucked in the poison of such blasphemies? What teacher delivered it to you? What learning moved you to think that the true King of Israel, that the veritable Son of God, would be He who would not suffer Himself to be crucified, and would set free His body from the fastenings of the nails? Not the hidden meaning of the Law, not the mouths of the Prophets. Had ye indeed ever read, I hid not my face from the shame of spitting; (Is. 50:6.) or that again, They pierced my hands and my feet, they told all my bones. (Ps. 22:16.) Where have ye ever read that the Lord came down from the cross? But ye have read, The Lord hath reigned from the tree.e
paragraphs.author: Leo the Great

paragraphs.text: But attend to this speech of these children of the Devil, how they imitate their father's speech. The Devil said, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down; (Matt. 4:6.) and they say now, If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Aha! is an interjection of taunt and mockery.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: Behold, there comes to mind what the Jews said in mockery to the crucified Son of God: "If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him." If he had then come down from the cross, yielding to the mockers, he would not have demonstrated to us the virtue of patience. But he waited a little, endured the insults, bore the ridicule, preserved his patience, and deferred their amazement; and he who was unwilling to come down from the cross rose from the tomb. Therefore it was a greater thing to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: It was a greater thing to destroy death by rising than to preserve life by coming down. But when the Jews did not see him come down from the cross at their taunts, when they saw him dying, they believed they had conquered him; they rejoiced that they had, as it were, extinguished his name. But behold, from his death his name has grown throughout the world—that death by which the faithless crowd believed they had extinguished it; and the one whose killing they celebrated, they now grieve as dead, because they recognize that he has attained his glory through suffering.
paragraphs.author: Gregory the Dialogist

paragraphs.text: (Verse 42.) He saved others, but he cannot save himself. Even unwillingly, the scribes and Pharisees confess that he saved others. Therefore, your own judgment condemns you. For if he, who saved others, had wanted to, he could have saved himself.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Even the Scribes and Pharisees reluctantly confess that He saved others. Your own judgment then condemns you, for in that He saved others, He could if He would have saved Himself.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But unworthy of credit is that promise, And we will believe him. For which is greater, to come down while yet alive from the cross, or to rise from the tomb when dead? Yet this He did, and ye believed not; therefore neither would ye have believed if He had come down from the cross. It seems to me that this was a suggestion of the dæmons. For immediately when the Lord was crucified they felt the power of the cross, and perceived that their strength was broken, and therefore contrive this to move Him to come down from the cross. But the Lord, aware of the designs of His foes, remains on the cross that He may destroy the Devil.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: (V. 43) If he is the king of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. He trusted in God; let Him deliver him now if He wants. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.' A fraudulent promise. What is more difficult, to come down from the cross while still alive, or to rise from the grave when dead? He has risen, and you did not believe. Therefore, even if he were to come down from the cross, you would not believe. But it seems to me that demons are sending him this message. For as soon as the Lord was crucified, they sensed the power of the cross and understood that their powers had been broken. And they are doing this in order for him to come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing the snares of his adversaries, remains on the cross to destroy the devil.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Wherefore they said those things, and also these. If "He is the king of Israel, let Him come down now from the cross. He saved others, Himself He cannot save," aiming hereby to bring discredit even on His former miracles. And again, "If He be Son of God, and He will have Him, let Him save Him."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: O execrable; most execrable! What, were not the prophets prophets, nor the righteous men righteous, because God rescued them not out of their dangers. Nay surely they were, though suffering these things. What then could be equal to your folly? For if the coming of the dangers upon them did not injure their honor with you, how much more in the case of this man, was it wrong for you to be offended, when both by what He did, by what He said, He was ever correcting beforehand this suspicion of yours.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: Yet nevertheless, even when these things were said and done, they prevailed nothing, not even at the very time. At any rate, he, who was depraved in such great wickedness, and who had spent his whole life in murders and house-breakings, when these things were being said, then confessed Him, and made mention of a kingdom, and the people bewailed Him. And yet the things that were done seemed to testify the contrary in the eyes of those who knew not the mysterious dispensations, that He was weak and of no power, nevertheless truth prevailed even by the contrary things.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: (V. 43) If he is the king of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. He trusted in God; let Him deliver him now if He wants. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.' A fraudulent promise. What is more difficult, to come down from the cross while still alive, or to rise from the grave when dead? He has risen, and you did not believe. Therefore, even if he were to come down from the cross, you would not believe. But it seems to me that demons are sending him this message. For as soon as the Lord was crucified, they sensed the power of the cross and understood that their powers had been broken. And they are doing this in order for him to come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing the snares of his adversaries, remains on the cross to destroy the devil.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: O execrable; most execrable! What, were not the prophets prophets, nor the righteous men righteous, because God rescued them not out of their dangers. Nay surely they were, though suffering these things. What then could be equal to your folly? For if the coming of the dangers upon them did not injure their honor with you, how much more in the case of this man, was it wrong for you to be offended, when both by what He did, by what He said, He was ever correcting beforehand this suspicion of yours.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: (de Cons. Ev. iii. 16.) It may seem that Luke contradicts this, when he describes one of the robbers as reviling Him, and as therefore rebuked by the other. But we may suppose that Matthew, shortly alluding to the circumstance, has used the plural for the singular, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we have, Hare stopped the months of lions, (Heb. 11:33.) when Daniel only is spoken of. And what more common way of speaking than for one to say, See the country people insult me, when it is one only who has done so. If indeed Matthew had said that both the thieves had reviled the Lord, there would be some discrepancy; but when he says merely, The thieves, without adding 'both,' we must consider it as that common form of speech in which the singular is signified by the plural.
paragraphs.author: Augustine of Hippo

paragraphs.text: That both the thieves cast in His teeth the manner of His Passion, shows that the cross should be an offence to all mankind, even to the faithful.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 44) Now even the robbers who were crucified with him were reviling him. Here, in a figurative sense known as σύλληψις, both robbers are depicted as blaspheming him. However, Luke asserts that while one blasphemed, the other confessed, and contrary to expectations, rebuked the blasphemer (Luke 23). It is not that the Gospels are inconsistent; rather, both robbers initially blasphemed, but then, as the sun set and the earth shook, and with rocks splitting and darkness descending, one believed in Jesus and rectified his previous denial with a subsequent confession. Among the two thieves, both the Gentiles and the Jews initially blasphemed the Lord. Later, one of them, struck by the magnitude of the signs, repented and to this day scolds the Jews for blaspheming.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Or it may be said that at first both reviled Him; but when the sun had withdrawn, the earth was shaken, the rocks were rent, and the darkness increased, one believed on Jesus, and repaired his former denial by a subsequent confession.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: Or, in the two thieves both nations, Jews and Gentiles, at first blasphemed the Lord; afterwards the latter terrified by the multitude of signs did penitence, and thus rebukes the Jews, who blaspheme to this day.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: At first both reviled Him, but afterwards not so. For that you should not suppose that the thing was arranged by any collusion, and that the thief was not a thief, he shows you by his wanton reproaches, that even after he was crucified he was a thief and a foe, but was afterwards totally changed.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Yet nevertheless, even when these things were said and done, they prevailed nothing, not even at the very time. At any rate, he, who was depraved in such great wickedness, and who had spent his whole life in murders and house-breakings, when these things were being said, then confessed Him, and made mention of a kingdom, and the people bewailed Him. And yet the things that were done seemed to testify the contrary in the eyes of those who knew not the mysterious dispensations, that He was weak and of no power, nevertheless truth prevailed even by the contrary things.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 87

paragraphs.text: And the robbers who were crucified with him reproached him with the same thing.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And in commenting on John we have explained, as best we could, concerning the two robbers who were crucified with Christ, who according to Matthew indeed and Mark both reproached him on the cross, but according to Luke, who says that "one of the hanging robbers blasphemed him, saying: You are the Christ; save yourself and us. But the other, answering, rebuked him, saying: Do you not fear God, seeing that you are in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive things worthy of our deeds; but this man has done nothing evil. And he said to Jesus: Remember me when you come into your kingdom. But Jesus, answering, said to him who had rebuked the one blaspheming: "Amen I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It is fitting, therefore, that at first indeed both robbers should be understood to have blasphemed the Lord, but after this that one of them was converted and believed, pondering within himself both about these miracles which he heard had been done by him, and perhaps also seeing the change of the air and the darkness that came about, unusual and not such as was frequently accustomed to happen.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or perhaps, as we said in that place too, these two robbers are different — of whom one was blaspheming him while the other rebuked the one blaspheming — and different were those two robbers who both blasphemed.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But that robber who was saved can be a mystery of those who after many iniquities believed in Christ and said: We have been crucified together with Christ and conformed to the death of Christ, and who always say to the Son of God: "Remember" us "when you come into your kingdom, and therefore" they are "in paradise" with him.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The thief who was saved may be a sign of those who after many sins have believed on Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now a certain Phlegon, a philosopher among the Greeks, recollects this darkness as an incredible occurrence in the fourteenth [night] of the moon, when an eclipse should not have appeared … for eclipses occur at the time when these two stars [the sun and the moon] draw near to one another. An eclipse of the sun happens at the conjunction of the sun and the moon as it runs into its way. This is not the time of the full moon, when the sun is diametrically opposed to the moon. But the eclipse occurred as creation mourned over what had happened, signifying that the drunken behavior of the Jews was linked to a darkened mind. The sunshine of the intellect had departed from them. For if they had been considering him—for that darkness found its source in the wrathful one and was evidence of what was about to overtake the murderers.
paragraphs.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

paragraphs.text: (Verse 45) But at the sixth hour, darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour. Those who wrote against the Gospels suspect a solar eclipse, which usually occurs at certain fixed times, as the reason for the disciples of Christ being misunderstood about the resurrection of the Lord: since a solar eclipse only occurs when the moon is rising. However, there is no doubt that during the time of Passover, the moon was full. And so it would not seem that the shadow of the earth, or the opposite side of the moon, made brief and rusty darkness, is placed in a space of three hours, so that every opportunity of causing harm is removed.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And I think this was done in order to fulfill the prophecy, saying: The sun shall go down at noon, and it shall be dark over the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9); and in another place: The sun went down while it was still day (Jeremiah 15:9). And it seems to me that the most radiant light of the world, that is, the greater luminary, withdrew its rays so as not to see the Lord hanging, or so that the wicked blasphemers might not enjoy their own light.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: This is the sign which before He had promised to give them when they asked it, saying, "An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign, and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas;" meaning His cross, and His death, His burial, and His resurrection. And again, declaring in another way the virtue of the cross, He said, "When ye have lifted up the Son of Man, then shall ye know that I am He." And what He saith is to this purport: "When ye have crucified me, and think ye have overcome me, then, above all, shall ye know my might."
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: For after the crucifixion, the city was destroyed, and the Jewish state came to an end, they fell away from their polity and their freedom, the gospel flourished, the word was spread abroad to the ends of the world; both sea and land, both the inhabited earth and the desert perpetually proclaim its power. These things then He meaneth, and those which took place at the very time of the crucifixion. For indeed it was much more marvellous that these things should be done, when He was nailed to the cross, than when He was walking on earth. And not in this respect only was the wonder, but because from heaven also was that done which they had sought, and it was over all the world, which had never before happened, but in Egypt only, when the passover was to be fulfilled. For indeed those events were a type of these.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: And observe when it took place. At midday, that all that dwell on the earth may know it, when it was day all over the world; which was enough to convert them, not by the greatness of the miracle only, but also by its taking place in due season. For after all their insulting, and their lawless derision, this is done, when they had let go their anger, when they had ceased mocking, when they were satiated with their jeerings, and had spoken all that they were minded; then He shows the darkness, in order that at least so (having vented their anger) they may profit by the miracle. For this was more marvellous than to come down from the cross, that being on the cross He should work these things.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: For whether they thought He Himself had done it, they ought to have believed and to have feared; or whether not He, but the Father, yet thereby ought they to have been moved to compunction, for that darkness was a token of His anger at their crime. For that it was not an eclipse, but both wrath and indignation, is not hence alone manifest, but also by the time, for it continued three hours, but an eclipse takes place in one moment of time, and they know it, who have seen this; and indeed it hath taken place even in our generation.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: And how, you may say, did not all marvel, and account Him to be God? Because the race of man was then held in a state of great carelessness and vice. And this miracle was but one, and when it had taken place, immediately passed away; and no one was concerned to inquire into the cause of it, and great was the prejudice and the habit of ungodliness. And they knew not what was the cause of that which took place, and they thought perhaps this happened so, in the way of an eclipse or some natural effect. And why dost thou marvel about them that are without, that knew nothing, neither inquired by reason of great indifference, when even those that were in Judaea itself, after so many miracles, yet continued using Him despitefully, although He plainly showed them that He Himself wrought this thing.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: And from the sixth hour there was darkness over the whole earth until the ninth hour. From this text certain people malign the truth of the Gospel, saying: how can what is said be true according to the text, namely that there was darkness over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth, since no history records that this happened? And they say that, just as usually happens in an eclipse of the sun, so an eclipse of the sun occurred at that time.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now an eclipse of the sun has always occurred throughout the ages at its own time. But the eclipse of the sun which is wont to happen according to the customary course of the seasons as they run does not occur at any other time than at the conjunction of the sun and the moon, when the moon, running beneath, obstructs the rays of the sun by coming to meet it, and by its encounter blunts its light. But at the time when Christ suffered it is manifest that there was no conjunction of the moon with the sun, since it was the Passover season, which is customary to keep when the moon has the fullness of the sun and is present the whole night.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: How then could there be an eclipse of the sun, when the moon was full and had the fullness of the sun?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But certain believers, wishing to introduce some defense against these arguments, hard pressed by the words of those who professed such things, spoke thus: if no new portent had happened at the time of Christ's passion but everything according to custom, it would be believed that that eclipse of the sun had happened according to custom; but now, since it is established that the other portents which happened then did not happen according to custom, but were new and wondrous (for indeed "the veil of the temple was torn into two parts from top to bottom, and the earth quaked, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened and many bodies of the sleeping saints rose again"), it is manifest that that eclipse of the sun too, consequently, in keeping with the other new portents, happened contrary to custom. Again, against these things the "sons of this age" who are "wiser than the sons of light in their generation" say such things as this: grant that that eclipse of the sun happened contrary to custom at a time not ancient, under the rule of the Romans, so that darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour — how is it that no one of the Greeks, no one of the barbarians, recorded that so marvelous a thing had happened at that time, especially those who wrote and noted chronicles, whenever any such new thing ever happened, but only your authors have written this? And a certain Phlegon wrote in his Chronicles that it happened in the rule of Tiberius Caesar, but he did not indicate that this happened at the full moon.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: See therefore whether this objection is not strong and able to move every wise man (who agrees neither with those who say these things nor with those who write those things, but hears everything with reason and judgment), and it is indeed not hard … and every one of the faithful (who indeed believes, yet does not believe with reason and with judgment), so that he may be so constant in faith that, even if they bring a thousand charges against the faith of the Gospel wishing to destroy our faith, he may in no part of them be shaken by the words of those who (pretending to believe the Gospel scriptures) through the occasion of one or another question, whether difficult or perhaps even insoluble, opposing the scriptures, hasten to take away the faith of Christ and of his Gospels from our soul, introducing certain moral matters and wishing to transfer the wonders accomplished by the power of God to certain secular customs.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: I have therefore judged it good, taking up the good purpose of those who desire to be constant in the faith, to find solutions to their accusations (as far as there is power in me from God) on behalf of the truth of the Gospel, so that the faithful may be fortified in faith not only by simple faith, but also by the reason of faith.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: We say therefore that Matthew and Mark did not say that an eclipse of the sun then happened, and neither did Luke, according to very many copies which have it thus: "and it was about the sixth hour, and darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour, and the sun was darkened". But in certain copies it does not have: "darkness fell and the sun was darkened"; but thus: "darkness fell over the whole earth, the sun failing". And perhaps someone ventured (as though wishing to say something more manifest) to put, in place of: "and the sun was darkened", "the sun failing", supposing that the darkness could not have happened otherwise than by "the sun failing".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But I rather think that those who lie in wait for the Church of Christ altered this word, so that it read "darkness fell, the sun failing", in order that the Gospels might plausibly be refuted according to the contrivances of those wishing to refute them. I judge therefore that, just as the other signs which happened in his passion happened in Jerusalem only, so also the darkness was made over the whole earth of Judea only until the ninth hour. And the things I say happened in Jerusalem only are these: that "the veil of the temple was torn", that "the earth quaked", that "the rocks were split", that "the tombs were opened".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For neither outside Judea "were the rocks split", nor "were tombs opened" other than only those which were in Jerusalem or perhaps in the land of Judea, nor did any other "earth quake" then except the earth of Jerusalem — for it is nowhere recorded that every element of the earth quaked at that time, so that (for example) both those who were in Ethiopia and those in India and in Scythia should feel it (which, had it happened, would without doubt be found in some histories of those who wrote in chronicles any new events). Just as, therefore, when it is said "the earth quaked", this refers to the earth of Jerusalem or (if one wishes to extend it more widely) to the earth of Judea, so also the darkness that fell from the sixth hour until the ninth over the whole earth was made over the whole earth of Judea, or certainly over Jerusalem only. Thus, therefore, whoever understands it this way understands it without fault, so that he may not, wishing to display the greatness of the miracle, fall into the mockery of the wise of "this age", and work unbelief rather than faith in wise men.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But someone says against these things: if the darkness then over the whole earth of Judea and Jerusalem was not made from an eclipse of the sun but from another cause, show the cause. To such we answer this: first indeed, that the evangelists did not at all name the sun in this place, but only that darkness fell over the whole earth. If therefore darkness fell over the whole earth with the sun not named, without doubt it follows to understand that certain most dark clouds, and perhaps not one but many and very great ones, ran together over the earth of Judea and Jerusalem to cover the rays of the sun, and therefore deep darkness fell from the sixth hour until the ninth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But since we have come to such a place, we say, lest perhaps also the "palpable darkness" in Egypt was made in this manner for "three days", not from an eclipse of the sun, but either because dark clouds ran together into one, or because the air there then became thicker over the Egyptians only — for "to all the sons of Israel", as the scripture testifies, "there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For it is also impossible in an eclipse of the sun, which happens from the coming together of the moon to the sun, for darkness to be made for "three" continuous "days"; and it would be believed that there was some other cause of the darkness in Egypt, if the sun had even been named, or as though darkened at that time. But now the scripture of Exodus says nothing else except that "Moses stretched out his hand to heaven, and there was darkness and gloom and the rest over the whole land of Egypt for three days; and no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his bed for three days".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But as to my saying over the whole earth of Judea or Jerusalem, so that we may not understand every element of the earth, this is the proof, which is written in the third book of Kingdoms, where Obadiah the steward of Ahab said to Elijah: "what have I sinned, that you have given your servant into the hands of Ahab, that he may put me to death?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: As your God lives, if there is a nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you, and I said: he is not here, and he burned the kingdom and its regions, because he did not find you". For who would be so stony, reading these things, as to suppose that Ahab king of Israel sent into every nation of the world and into every kingdom of the whole earth seeking Elijah, and burned wherever it was said: Elijah is not here? But without doubt those things were said hyperbolically, showing that he sought him abundantly among the nations that were around Judea, according as he was able to seek. And we have said also in other places that, since two general creatures were made on the sixth day, first indeed the animals, and then man made "according to the image of God", it follows that that sixth day too should be understood as then having been divided into two kinds of creature, so that before the sixth hour the animals should be understood to have been created, but at the sixth hour the Lord said: "let us make man to our image" and made him then. … on which account it was fitting that, for the salvation of that same man, he who was dying should be hung up at that very sixth hour, and from the sixth hour for this reason the darkness should be made over the whole earth until the ninth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And just as, when Moses stretched out his hand "to heaven", "darkness was made over the Egyptians", who held the servants of God in servitude, an image of the future darkness which was to seize the Egyptians, similarly also when Christ at the sixth hour stretched out his hands on the cross to heaven over the people who had cried out: "take this man from the earth", and "crucify, crucify him", darkness was made, and they were deprived of all light.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And that darkness was an image of the future darkness which was to seize the Jewish nation, because they dared to lay their hands upon the true light.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Whence from that time all that nation has been filled with darkness, as the prophet says: "let their eyes be darkened that they may not see".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Likewise under Moses "there was darkness and gloom over the whole land of Egypt for three days; and no one saw his brother, nor did anyone rise from his bed for three days; but to all the sons of Israel there was light in all the places in which they were dwelling". But under Christ darkness fell over the whole earth of Judea for three hours, but there was light over all the rest of the earth. Which everywhere illumines the whole Church of God in Christ.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And if until the ninth hour there was darkness over the whole earth of Judea, it is manifest that light shone upon them again, because "when the multitude of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved". But that the darkness was made over the whole earth of Judea for three hours, this shows that on account of their sins they were deprived of the light of three hours: of the light of God the Father and of the splendor of Christ and of the illumination of the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Some take occasion from this text to cavil against the truth of the Gospel. For indeed from the beginning eclipses of the sun have happened in their proper seasons; but such an eclipse as would be brought about by the ordinary course of the seasons could only be at such time as the sun and moon come together, when the moon passing beneath intercepts the sun's rays. But at the time of Christ's passion it is clear that this was not the case, because it was the paschal feast, which it was customary to celebrate when the moon was full. Some believers, desiring to produce some answer to this objection, have said, that this eclipse in accordance with the other prodigies was an exception to the established laws of nature.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Against this the children of this world urge, How is it that of the Greeks and Barbarians, who have made observations of these things, not one has recorded so remarkable a phenomenon as this? Phlegon indeed has recorded such an event as happening in the time of Tiberius Caesar, but he has not mentioned that it was at the full moon. I think therefore that, like the other miracles which took place at the Passion, the rending of the veil, and the earthquake, this also was confined to Jerusalem.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or, if any one chooses, it may be extended to the whole of Judæa; as in the book of Kings, Abdias said to Elias, As the Lord thy God liveth, there is no nation or kingdom whither my lord hath not sent to seek thee, (1 Kings 18:10.) meaning that he had been sought in the countries round about Judæa.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Accordingly we might suppose many and dense clouds to have been brought together over Jerusalem and Judæa, enough to produce thick darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour. For we understand that there were two creatures created on the sixth day, the beasts before the sixth hour, man on the sixth; and therefore it was fitting that He who died for the salvation of man should be crucified at the sixth hour, and for this cause that darkness should be over the whole earth from the sixth to the ninth hour. And as by Moses stretching out his hands towards heaven darkness was brought upon the Egyptians who held the servants of God in bondage, so likewise when at the sixth hour Christ stretched out his hands on the cross to heaven, darkness came over all the people who had cried out, Crucify him, and they were deprived of all light as a sign of the darkness that should come, and that should envelop the whole people of the Jews. Further, under Moses there was darkness over the land of Egypt three days, but all the children of Israel had light; so under Christ there was darkness over all Judæa for three hours, because for their sins they were deprived of the light of God the Father, the splendour of Christ, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But over the rest of the earth there is light, which every where illumines the Church of God in Christ. And if to the ninth hour there was darkness over Judæa, it is manifest that light returned to them again after that; so, when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have entered in, then all Israel shall be saved. (Rom. 11:25.)
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Creation could not bear the outrage offered to the Creator; whence the sun withdrew his beams, that he might not look upon the crime of these impious men.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: (ad Polycarp. Ep. 7.) When we were together at Heliopolis, we both observed such an interference of the moon with the sun quite unexpectedly, for it was not the season of their conjunction; and then from the ninth hour until evening, beyond the power of nature, continuing in a direct line between us and the sun. And this obscuration we saw begin from the east, and so pass to the extreme of the sun's orb, and again return back the same way, being thus the very reverse of an ordinary eclipse.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite

paragraphs.text: But My People hath changed their glory: whence no profit shall accrue to them: the heaven turned pale thereat" (and when did it turn pale? undoubtedly when Christ suffered), "and shuddered," he says, "most exceedingly; " and "the sun grew dark at mid-day: " (and when did it "shudder exceedingly" except at the passion of Christ, when the earth also trembled to her centre, and the veil of the temple was rent, and the tombs were burst asunder? "because these two evils hath My People done; Me," He says, "they have quite forsaken, the fount of water of life, and they have digged for themselves worn-out tanks, which will not be able to contain water.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: And so the "pressure" must be maintained up to that hour in which the orb-involved from the sixth hour in a general darkness-performed for its dead Lord a sorrowful act of duty; so that we too may then return to enjoyment when the universe regained its sunshine. If this savours more of the spirit of Christian religion, while it celebrates more the glory of Christ, I am equally able, from the self-same order of events, to fix the condition of late protraction of the Station; (namely), that we are to fast till a late hour, awaiting the time of the Lord's sepulture, when Joseph took down and entombed the body which he had requested.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: Night following day marks a division of times. Thus is fulfilled the triad of days and nights, and the hidden mystery of God's work is perceived with astonishment by all of creation. The cry to God in truth is the voice of a body departing, having declared the separation of the Word of God from itself. He wonders why he is being abandoned when he exclaims, "God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" But he was forsaken because his humanity had to pass even through death.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: It must be considered carefully that he gave up the spirit with a loud cry after he drank from the sponge full of vinegar offered to him on a reed. Wine is the honor and power of immortality, but it soured through the fault of the vessel or through carelessness. Therefore, since this wine had soured in Adam, he himself accepted it and drank from the nations. The fact that it was offered to him to drink from a sponge on a reed signifies that he took from the bodies of the Gentiles the sins which had ruined eternity and transferred our sins to himself, uniting them to his immortality.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (de Trin. x. 50 &c.) From these words heretical spirits contend either that God the Word was entirely absorbed into the soul at the time it discharged the function of a soul in quickening the body; or that Christ could not have been born man, because the Divine Word dwelt in Him after the manner of a prophetical spirit.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: As though Jesus Christ was a man of ordinary soul and body, having His beginning then when He began to be man, and thus now deserted upon the withdrawal of the protection of God's word cries out, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Or at least that the nature of the Word being transmuted into soul, Christ, who had depended in all things upon His Father's support, now deserted and left to death, mourns over this desertion, and pleads with Him departing.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: But amidst these impious and feeble opinions, the faith of the Church imbued with Apostolic teaching does not sever Christ that He should be considered as Son of God and not as Son of Man. The complaint of His being deserted is the weakness of the dying man; the promise of Paradise is the kingdom of the living God. You have Him complaining that He is left to death, and thus He is Man; you have Him as He is dying declaring that He reigns in Paradise; and thus He is God. Wonder not then at the humility of these words, when you know the form of a servant, and see the offence of the cross.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 46.) And about the ninth hour, Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lammasabacthani, which means: My God, My God, why have you forsaken me? He made use of the beginning of the twenty-first psalm, and that which is read in the middle of the verse: Look upon me, for it is useless. For it is read in Hebrew: My God, My God, why have you forsaken me? Therefore, those who think that this psalm is spoken from the perspective of David, Esther, or Mordecai are wicked, since the evangelists also understand the testimonies taken from it concerning the Savior, as in: They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots. And another thing: They pierced my hands and my feet. Do not be surprised at the lowly words and the complaints of one who is forsaken, when you see the form of a servant and the scandal of the cross.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: He employed the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm. (Ps. 22:1. Vulg.) That clause in the middle of the verse, Look upon me, is superfluous; for the Hebrew has only 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani,' that is, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? It is impiety therefore to think that this Psalm was spoken in the character of David or Esther or Mardocheus, when passages taken out of it by the Evangelist are understood of the Saviour; as, They parted my garments among them, and, They pierced my hands.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: And for this reason, even after this He speaks, that they might learn that He was still alive, and that He Himself did this, and that they might become by this also more gentle, and He saith, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?" that unto His last breath they might see that He honors His Father, and is no adversary of God. Wherefore also He uttered a certain cry from the prophet, even to His last hour bearing witness to the Old Testament, and not simply a cry from the prophet, but also in Hebrew, so as to be plain and intelligible to them, and by all things He shows how He is of one mind with Him that begat Him.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: But it must be asked, What means this, that Christ is forsaken of God? Some, unable to explain how Christ could be forsaken of God, say that this was spoken out of humility. But you will be able clearly to comprehend His meaning if you make a comparison of the glory which He had with the Father with the shame which He despised when He endured the cross.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: When He saw darkness over the whole land of Judæa He said this, Father, why hast thou forsaken me? meaning, Why hast thou given Me over exhausted to such sufferings? that the people who were honoured by Thee may receive the things that they have dared against Me, and should be deprived of the light of Thy countenance. Also, Thou hast forsaken Me for the salvation of the Gentiles.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But what good have they of the Gentiles who have believed done, that I should deliver them from the evil one by shedding My precious blood on the ground for them? Or will they, for whom I suffer these things, ever do aught worthy of them? Or foreseeing the sins of those for whom He suffered, He said, Why hast thou forsaken me? that I should become as one that, gathereth stubble in the harvest, and gleanings in the vintage. (Mic. 7:1.) But you must not imagine that the Saviour said this after the manner of men by reason of the misery which encompassed Him on the cross; for if you take it so you will not hear His loud voice and mighty words which point to something great hidden.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Now about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lama sabacthani? that is: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? But those who were standing there and heard it said that this man is calling Elijah (27, 46. 47).
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: It must be inquired, in a manner worthy of the Lord, what that great voice of Christ was—whether great by reason of things signifying great mysteries, or great by the sensible and bodily hearing of a great voice. But I think that every voice of Christ, the Son of God, is great, even if it be soft; and Scripture bears witness to this very thing especially in those places in which it wishes to raise up the hearer, so that he may pass beyond that which many are able to understand in such passages, and may not remain in it (although according to the simple understanding it may have in it some truth), so that he may be able to understand something in a manner worthy on account of the great voice of the Lord. Since, therefore, by these words he shows that there is something hidden and great, when he cries out to God, saying, why hast thou forsaken me, therefore it must be inquired what it is that was forsaken by God. Christ; for it is not permissible to believe that he lies when he says: why have you forsaken me.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And some, out of a religious coloring on Jesus' behalf, and because they cannot explain what it means for Christ to be forsaken by God, suppose and say: it is indeed true what was said, yet it was said out of humility.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But we, seeing him who had been established "in the form of God" descending from a greatness of this kind and emptying himself through this, that he "took on the form of a servant", and seeing in these things the will of him who sent him to such conditions, understand that, as regards those things in which there had been the form of the invisible God and the image according to the Father, he was forsaken by the Father when he "took on the form of a servant", and he was forsaken for the sake of men, so that he might take on such and so great things, so that he might come "even unto death", "and the death of the cross", which among men is seen to be the most shameful.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For the extremity of his being forsaken came about when they crucified him and placed above his head, as if mocking him, letters saying: "this is Jesus the king of the Jews". And that too was an extremity of his being forsaken, that he was crucified among robbers, and that "those passing by blasphemed him, wagging their heads over him", and that the chief men with the scribes were saying: "he saved others, himself he cannot save", and still further that too, that "even the robbers reproached him" on the cross.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Therefore you will be able clearly to understand what it is that he says: why hast thou forsaken me? — making a comparison of that glory which he had with the Father to the confusion which, despising it, he endured on the cross. For his throne was "as the sun in the sight of God, and as the perfect moon for ever; and his witness in heaven was faithful".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But afterward, for those on whose behalf he says: why hast thou forsaken me, he added further, saying: "but thou hast repelled and brought to nothing, and hast put off thy Christ, thou hast overthrown the covenant of thy servant, thou hast profaned his holiness upon the earth", and the rest. And so long as there was light from the sun, even while enduring such great and such grievous things He did not say Why hast Thou forsaken Me?; but after He saw that darkness had come "over all the land of Judaea until the ninth hour," He said with His great voice Why hast Thou forsaken Me, wishing to show by these words this: that Thou hast forsaken Me willingly, Father, and hast delivered Me up, emptied out, to such calamities, in order that the people who had been held in honor with Thee might receive what it dared to do against Me — filling up the "measure of its fathers," and the things it did against the prophets — so that it might be deprived of the light of Thy watchful care and be brought into darkness, as though Thou, O God, wert now in no way present with them. But also for the salvation of the Gentiles Thou hast forsaken Me, that by the "trespass" of Israel there might come "the salvation of the Gentiles." Yet what so good a thing did those who believed from among the Gentiles do, that with My "precious blood" poured out upon the earth for them I should purchase them from the evil one who had held them fast? And why hast Thou "turned away Thy face, and I have become troubled," so that I say: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death"?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or what such worthy thing are those men going to do, for whom I suffer these things, that I should suffer these things for them? — even as the prophet also foretold beforehand concerning this very thing, as though crying out to Thee and saying: "What profit," Father, has been made to men "in My blood, while I go down into corruption?
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Shall the dust confess to Thee, or shall it declare Thy truth?" But perhaps also, seeing the sins of the men for whom He was suffering, He said: Why hast Thou forsaken Me, that I should become "like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, and like one who gleans grapes in the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat of the first-fruits?" And these things I say, "because the God-fearing man has perished from the earth, and there is none who sets right among men." Wherefore do not suppose that the Savior said these things after the manner of men, because of the calamity that had laid hold of Him upon the cross.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For if thou takest it so, thou wilt not be one who hears the great voice in which He spoke these things, nor wilt thou seek things worthy of a divine voice. Therefore "the darkness indeed was made from the sixth hour over the whole earth until the ninth"; but before the ninth hour was ended, the Lord cried out about it with a loud voice, saying the things that are written, as if demanding that the sun of the earth should rise, dissolving in her the darkness of the three hours according to what we have set forth above.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Or, The Saviour said this as bearing about with Him our feelings, who when placed in dangers think ourselves forsaken by God. Human nature was forsaken by God because of its sins, and the Son of God becoming our Advocate laments the misery of those whose guilt He took upon Himf; there in showing how they who sin ought to mourn, when He who never sinned did thus mourn.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: We have, moreover, in that other Gospel a clear revelation, i.e. of the Son's distinction from the Father, "My God, why hast Thou forsaken me? " and again, (in the third Gospel,) "Father, into Thy hands I commend my spirit.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: He exclaims that God had forsaken Him. He commends His spirit into the hands of the Father.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: However, if you persist in pushing your views further, I shall find means of answering you with greater stringency, and of meeting you with the exclamation of the Lord Himself, so as to challenge you with the question, What is your inquiry and reasoning about that? You have Him exclaiming in the midst of His passion: "My God, my God, why hast Thou forsaken me? " Either, then, the Son suffered, being "forsaken" by the Father, and the Father consequently suffered nothing, inasmuch as He forsook the Son; or else, if it was the Father who suffered, then to what God was it that He addressed His cry? But this was the voice of flesh and soul, that is to say, of man-not of the Word and Spirit, that is to say, not of God; and it was uttered so as to prove the impassibility of God, who "forsook" His Son, so far as He handed over His human substance to the suffering of death.
paragraphs.author: Tertullian

paragraphs.text: (Verse 47.) But some of those standing there, when they heard it, said: This man is calling Elijah. Not all, but some whom I believe were Roman soldiers, not understanding the nature of the Hebrew language, but from what he said: Eli, Eli, thinking that he was calling Elijah. But if we want to understand the Jews who said this, they do this in their usual way, to dishonor the Lord of weakness, who invokes the aid of Elijah.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: It follows, Some of them that stood by, &c.; some, not all; whom I suppose to have been Roman soldiers, ignorant of Hebrew, but from the words Eli, Eli, thought that He called upon Elias. But if we prefer to suppose them Jews, they do it after their usual manner, that they may accuse the Lord of weakness in thus invoking Elias.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But some standing there and hearing him said: This man is calling Elijah … but the others said: Let us see whether Elijah comes and delivers him.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: As though they had heard that he called upon God, and had marveled at his prayer on the cross, greater than was the prayer of Jonah praying in the belly of the whale, and had been profited by it, so that even when set amid the most extreme calamities they might not cease to pray to God. And I say that the prayer of Christ was greater than that of Jonah in the belly of the whale on account of the magnitude of the things that are shown forth from it, and on account of the great effect of his voluntary passion.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: The soldiers misunderstanding the sound of the Lord's words, foolishly looked for the coming of Elias. But God, whom the Saviour thus invoked in the Hebrew tongue, He had ever inseparably with Him.
paragraphs.author: Rabanus Maurus

paragraphs.text: Vinegar is wine, which has turned sour either from neglect, or the fault of the vessel. Wine is the honour of immortality, or virtue. When this then had been turned sour in Adam, He took and drunk it at the hands of the Gentiles. It is offered to Him on a reed and a spunge; that is, He took from the bodies of the Gentiles immortality spoiled and corrupted, and transfused in Himself into a mixture of immortality that in us which was spoiled.
paragraphs.author: Hilary of Poitiers

paragraphs.text: (Verse 48.) And immediately one of them, running, filled a sponge with vinegar and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink. And these things were done so that the prophecy would be fulfilled: They gave me vinegar for my thirst (Psalms 68:22). Even to this day, the Jews and all the unbelievers give Jesus vinegar and gall to drink on the Sunday of his resurrection; and they give him wine mixed with myrrh to make him sleepy, so that he does not see their evil.
paragraphs.author: Jerome

paragraphs.text: But mark herein also their wantonness, and intemperance, and folly. They thought (it is said) that it was Elias whom He called, and straightway they gave Him vinegar to drink. But another came unto Him, and "pierced His side with a spear." What could be more lawless, what more brutal, than these men; who carried their madness to so great a length, offering insult at last even to a dead body?
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: But mark thou, I pray thee, how He made use of their wickednesses for our salvation. For after the blow the fountains of our salvation gushed forth from thence.
paragraphs.author: John Chrysostom
paragraphs.work: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 88

paragraphs.text: And perhaps all who know the ecclesiastical doctrine, but live amiss, have given them to drink wine mingled with gall; but they who attribute to Christ untrue opinions, these filling a sponge with vinegar, put it upon the reed of Scripture, and put it to His mouth.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And immediately one of them ran up, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink. And thus he fulfilled in himself the prophecy that spoke of him: "and they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: For this reason too, according to John, when Jesus had received the vinegar with the gall, he said: "it is finished" — this also, which the Scripture had foretold concerning me. And one may with pleasure apply this text against those who have written or do write malicious things against Christ, of whom Isaiah says: "woe to those who write malicious things; for in writing they write malicious things" (I speak of those who have left behind certain writings, speaking "iniquity on high"). And one will use this text when he sees them gathering from certain things they have heard — whether of heathen sayings or of barbarous discourses — and composing a narrative like a kind of sponge, filling it not with any drinkable word nor with wine that gladdens "the heart of man" nor with the water of "refreshment", but with a kind of contrary and harmful and undrinkable intelligible vinegar; and this sponge they put upon the reed of their own writing and (so far as in them lies) inflict injuries upon Jesus by a drink of this kind. And some indeed give Jesus "wine mingled with gall to drink", which Jesus the Son of God will not drink, but others give not wine but vinegar.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: And perhaps those who, so far as ecclesiastical doctrine is concerned, have right understanding, but live wickedly, give him "wine mingled with gall to drink"; while those who apply to Christ wisdoms alien from the truth, as though he were speaking them, these fill a sponge with vinegar, put it upon a reed, and give him to drink.
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But there are also those who, as John writes, "offer to his mouth both vinegar and gall". And perhaps those who merely have wrong understanding fill a sponge with vinegar and put it upon the reed of their own writing and give him to drink; but those who both understand wrongly concerning the dispensations of Christ and live wickedly, these, "putting a sponge full of vinegar with gall and hyssop" upon the reed of their writing, offer it "to his mouth".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: But he who will not even drink his "wine" because of the admixture of gall, will much more not drink "vinegar", nor "vinegar mingled with gall". Therefore let us, receiving from our Savior Jesus himself (who is the "true vine") wine pure from all sharpness and bitterness, wine which "gladdens the heart of man" and the heart of the Son of God himself, give him and his disciples to drink of it, so that he may say of us who give him and his disciples good drink: "I thirsted and you gave me drink". Let us also receive the "water of refreshment" with which "the good shepherd" nourishes the just, so that those who are fed by him may say: "he brought us up beside the water of refreshment".
paragraphs.author: Origen of Alexandria

paragraphs.text: Thus the Source of living water is made to drink vinegar, the Giver of honey is fed with gall; Forgiveness is scourged, Acquittance is condemned, Majesty is mocked, Virtue ridiculed, the Bestower of showers is repaid with spitting.
paragraphs.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: Or otherwise; The Jews as degenerating from the wine of the Patriarchs and Prophets were vinegar; they had deceitful hearts, like to the winding holes and hollows in spunge. By the reed, Sacred Scripture is denoted, which was fulfilled in this action; for as we call that which the tongue utters, the Hebrew tongue, or the Greek tongue, for example; so the writing, or letters which the seed produces, we may call a reed.
paragraphs.author: Remigius of Rheims

paragraphs.text: This is also the beginning of the translation of souls into the heavens. For whatever souls follow Christ are translated. Stephen made this plain when he said, "Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit." Paul also writes, "It is better to depart and be with Christ." Such was not the case with those of ancient times.
